A new method is given for categorizing spaces according to their reversible characteristics. These categories are based on a set of principles similar to those used in the waterfall framework. Each space is assigned a label consisting of a tuple of integers, representing the space's homotopy groups at successive stages of a filtration. This label captures key information about the space as constructed from a sequence of operations, which can be interpreted as a sequence of homotopy surgeries. It's proven that two spaces with the same label have equivalent properties if and only if they are homotopically equivalent. Furthermore, it's demonstrated that the filteration label captures a broad range of distinct topological properties. As a consequence, the number of possible labels corresponds to a lower bound on the number of topological properties. This approach is illustrated by labeling spaces in the Reeb-Wheeler framework for manifolds and CW-complexes and the Cech chain complex framework for spaces with a given covering. Both the standard and non-standard labels for a particular space are examined. Finally, the standard framework spaces of all groups are generated using the GroupPy group theory library and the PyHomotopy pipeline. The computations demonstrate that the number of distinct labels for groups with a given order is proportional to the order, indicating that there may be significantly more topological properties than classes of equivalences. Future research plans are outlined, including applying the method in algebraic topology and extending the method to measure properties of 2-group manifolds. The code used for these computations is publicly available at https://github.com/tyrrell13/group-py. Each framework label corresponds to a unique group up to reversal. The following equivalence relations are confirmed through the computations: ${\bf Z}_{128} \sim {\bf Z}_{127}^{n}$ for $n=1,2$, and ${\bf Z}_{128} \sim {\bf Z}_{128}^{n}$ for $n=2,3$. To obtain this information, we employ two advanced ASR methods: (1) a language model-driven approach to consider various word predictions as uncertainties, and (two) a top-N best path encoding that captures the probability distribution among these predictions. Furthermore, our approach aligns with recent scalable neural state monitoring techniques. Although our work is primarily focused on dialogue state monitoring, the proposed method is versatile and can be applied to other NLP models as well. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall firing activity within the network. By assuming random connections, we analyze the impacts of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on network dynamics, examining the effects of introducing a specified number of nodes with extreme in- and out-degrees. Our findings reveal that more uneven degree distributions can lead to improved theta neuron performance and higher firing rates. Ultimately, we investigate the interplay between the strength of synaptic connections and network node pairing.  This work is an initial exploration into applying statistical mechanics principles to biological networks, focusing on the effects of degree distribution widths on theta neuron dynamics.  Due to the limitations of the random synapse model, we cannot delve into the role of specific connections, thereby recommending similar future studies to investigate more structured network scenarios.  One potential extension could involve evaluating the behavior of networks composed of excitatory and inhibitory neurons to see if this distinction influences the dynamics of degree distribution widths.  Our analysis suggests that examining the impacts of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths is a crucial step in understanding theta neuron behavior and offers an additional control parameter to manipulate network behavior beyond connection strength and neuron excitability.  These findings may be relevant for biological neural networks, potentially serving as an initial step in developing a more comprehensive theory that links the functionality of individual neurons to that of the entire neural system. Automated Program Repair (APR) is a rapidly evolving area of research aimed at automatically fixing concisely specified program bugs. While successful in a few small languages, the approach remains poorly performing in more broadly used programming languages. One challenge is the tendency for APR tools to suggest a multitude of fixes for a single bug before finding one. In order to improve the outcome for more broadly used languages, we investigate a novel strategy called antagonistic patch creation. By quickly generating multiple antagonistic patches for each bug, the probability of a correct fix being proposed is increased. We evaluate this approach on 1,000 real bugs from the 12 standard input languages at the 15th edition of the Defects4J dataset. In comparison to the state-of-the-art repair tool, AST-GHAST, our approach significantly enhances the outcome by 3.2 times and achieves an average time efficiency that is 3.4 times faster. The implementation of our approach is available for public use.

In recent years, particularly concerning crime-related issues, time series analysis has been a key focus in statistics and machine learning research, aiming to better understand and make accurate predictions.  From a statistical perspective, specifically with regards to cluster analysis, this paper seeks to provide an in-depth analysis of homicide rates in a selected Brazilian region, exploring the underlying causes and assuming that these factors will persist in the future to inform relevant public policy decisions.  Moreover, this study aims to compare how well machine learning and traditional statistical methods can forecast homicide rates, evaluating the performance of Accordo's, King's and Han and Tiao's models against a dataset spanning 13 years.  Specifically, this research utilizes annual homicide rate data across 18 municipalities in Goias, spanning from 2002 to 2014, for a total sample size of 182.  First, the time series are visually evaluated through Plots of $(y_{t}-y_{t-4},y_{t}-y_{t-1})$ and tested for equality in second and fourth moments, revealing non-degenerate fourth moment effects.  Next, the time series are clustered based on their correlation matrices, applying the Hierarchical Agglomeration method and topological measures to group 18 municipalities into 5 clusters.  This research finds that the clustered municipalities share characteristics such as geographical proximity, shared border municipalities, contiguity and demographic similarity, revealing that the municipalities in Goias can be divided into five groups: (i) Municipalities surrounding the capital city of Goias $(n=4$); (ii) The Sudoeste Goias cluster $(n=6$); (iii) The Norte Goias cluster $(n=3$); (iv) Leste Goias $(n=4$) and (v) Centro-Norte Goias cluster $(n=5$).  The chapter concludes by evaluating the performance of seasonal adjustment methods on non-degenerate fourth moment time series, comparing the accuracy of Accordo's, King's and Han and Tiao's models against an in-sample baseline, and highlighting Goias' capital city of Goias as a significant outlier in homicide rate forecasting.  Ultimately, this research recommends increased investment in socio-economical infrastructura by the sudoeste Goias cluster $(n=6$) and promoting actions aimed at reducing armed gun ownership, observed in centro-norte Goias cluster $(n=5$).  Such investment could potentially boost Goias' overall economic development, contributing to a decrease in homicide rates.

Optimizing machine learning models through the stochastic gradient descent process can be hindered by learning rate suboptimal choices. Selecting an inappropriate learning rate can cause convergence to a point from which the optimizer makes no progress. Conversely, an optimal learning rate allows the optimizer to efficiently explore the parameter search space, rapidly converging towards a optimal solution. 
A number of algorithms have been developed to facilitate accelerated stochastic gradient descent convergence, such as Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent and Polyak's heavy ball methods. These algorithms were initially designed with certain properties in mind: uniform stability and a global Lipschitzness. However, real-world optimization tasks increasingly demonstrate non-uniform stability and a lack of global Lipschitzness, as evidenced by class imbalance problems where different classes contribute differently to the optimization process, resulting in varied convergence rates. 
This research aims to bridge the gap between existing accelerated SGD algorithms and real-world optimization tasks by developing a new family of algorithms. These new tools will exhibit improved convergence speed properties even in the absence of uniform stability and a global Lipschitzness guarantee. A novel approach to this problem is to utilize a new class of quadratic functions in the optimization process, allowing for a single iteration complexity of $O(\sqrt{m})$ and an accelerated complexity of $O(m)$. These new quadratic Bregman divergence-based algorithms guarantee improved convergence, with a single iteration complexity of $m$ in the absence of a uniform stability guarantee and a global Lipschitzness guarantee. 
To validate these new algorithms, two test cases were employed: a standard optimization test case with known parameters and an optimization test case mimicking real-world data, complete with optimizations aimed at reducing feature dominance. Various comparative algorithms were used to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, including baseline optimizers like vanilla SGD and its weighted variants, accelerated SGD and its weighted variants, and other non-base optimizers like gradient descent with a F1 metric. 
When tested against these comparisons, the proposed algorithms exhibited improved convergence properties in both test cases: an optimized complexity of $m$ in the standard test case and a reduced feature dominance complexity of $\sqrt{m}$ in the second test case. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms and their potential applications in optimization problems, especially those mimicking real-world data.

In many dryland ecosystems around the world, overgrazing poses a significant threat due to its prolonged and irreversible consequences which lead to erosion and soil degradation. While non-resident grazing is becoming a more prevalent management approach in some areas, there is still a significant shortage of scientific research regarding its effects compared to resident grazing. This study employed a novel agent-based model that takes into account individual animal behavior in relation to food scarcity and vegetation density to investigate the impact of both resident and non-resident grazing on the dynamics of plants. We discovered through our simulations that non-resident grazing is more likely to maintain a balance between plants and their environment in comparison to resident grazing. Additionally, a theoretical model was developed that highlighted the complex interplay of factors such as non-resident grazing frequency, travel distance, resource allocation, food scarcity, and vegetation density as key determinants that impact dynamics. We found through our simulations that a specific range of grazing frequency and travel distances can result in self-sustaining patterns of balanced plant growth. We ultimately validated our findings by comparing them to existing research on overgrazing and suggested that non-resident grazing could serve as an effective method for mitigating soil degradation and promoting sustainable environmental balance. The main limitation of our study lies in the assumption that each grazing head has equal access to food which may not reflect the natural behavior of animals. This study could contribute significantly to the development of effective conservation strategies in dryland ecosystems through its employ of various methodologies including scientific research, sustainability principles, and system dynamics. While our study primarily focuses on non-resident grazing, its broader implications can be applied to various grazing models that aim to inform effective conservation practices. The model source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/arhamhanif/Non-Resident-Grazing Model. The model comprises three distinct components, namely, Plant Model, Grazing Model, and Geographic Information System. Plant Model serves as the primary component that deals with dryland plant dynamics while Grazing Model entails the behavior of grazers in relation to food scarcity and vegetation density. The Geographic Information System, on the other hand, enables the simulation of non-resident grazing frequency and travel distances to investigate their impact on balanced plant growth. The model utilizes a combination of agent-based modeling and system dynamics, and its key features can be explored in the provided repository. A popular dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs random linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space by assigning a counter to each dimension. It is well-suited for handling distributions with significant support, but its performance against specialized attackers that can manipulate the distribution is poorly understood. This paper explores the resistance of CountSketch against such adversaries, revealing a surprising resilience: Admirable performance persists even when the adversary has knowledge of the distribution and can adapt to the user's random linear measurements. Specifically, we show that these adversaries can only marginally decrease the success probability, namely, the attacker can reduce the probability by at most logarithmic factor. Abstractive summarization and condensation techniques can't rely on pre-defined templates to generate summaries because they frequently miss crucial details. Entity-based prompts have been shown to enhance the accuracy of low-shot and few-shot models in these fields by allowing the model to learn entity-related keywords. In this research, we test the efficacy of acquiring entity-related keywords through a planning process and use them as prompts to enhance the accuracy of low-shot models in abstractive condensation and summarization tasks. Our method employs planning heuristics that ensure the prompt includes all the entities required to meet the task's objectives. We derive our heuristics from existing rules relevant to the task and utilize rule-based learning algorithms to identify the specific rules that result in the most accurate condensations when used as prompts. When evaluated on the TAC2010 and TAC2011 datasets, our method significantly enhances the ROUGE performance of the top-shots of the strong BART model from 10.25 to 12.85, increasing it to the level of its few-shot counterpart. Additionally, when evaluated on real-world datasets, our method results in condensations that are preferred by human evaluators 54% of the time, matching the preference of our few-shot baseline. The methodology also involves determining the feature type at the surface's pole point, calculating a radius parameter, and scaling a spherical surface to match the measured point cloud data's feature type, curvature, and size while minimizing the sum of squared errors. Evolutionary algorithms have seen an increase in efficiency when parallel processing was incorporated, leading to enhanced variants like PMSO.  Despite improvements, PMSO may experience lower convergence speed compared to solo runners when employing a first-to-complete approach due to time disparity among individuals.  This time disparity can cause those who complete evolution earliest to dominate parent selection, potentially leading to a lack of exploration for non-converged solutions, thus restricting their possibilities.  This research presents a unique approach called FOPS - a variant of PMSO that eliminates the effect of time disparity by a modified parent selection strategy.  Instead of taking completion time into consideration, FOPS considers how well individuals have progressed towards convergence, as measured by fitness change, for solution evaluation and parent selection.  Those with the greatest change in fitness are given priority, thus enabling all individuals to have an equal chance at parent selection, independent of the evolution progress pace.  Compared to traditional PMSO, the proposed FOPS exhibits faster convergence and more potential solutions over a range of numerical test functions and realistic high-dimensional scenarios.  Moreover, the effectiveness of FOPS is validated through a K-Means clustering algorithm and a real-world multi-objective optimization problem.  The empirical outcomes demonstrate that addressing the time disparity gap can significantly contribute to enhancing the performance of parallel evolutionary algorithms and related variants.  Consequently, the use of convergence progress instead of completion time for evaluation is a valuable contribution to the evolution strategies research community. the training process is heavily dominated by matrix inversions, which are

technique that involves parallelizing matrix inversions without affecting the model's accuracy. Specifically, we have implemented high-parallelism training using TPUs for LMNs, which has yielded a notable two-day reduction in training time. In a groundbreaking experiment, our team has successfully demonstrated the concept of irreversible optical nonreversible work (ONR). An optical system is used here instead of the more conventional electrical systems. Building upon the idea of free-energy withdrawal, ONR occurs when a device is driven out of its equilibrium state due to a change in entropy. Unlike the standard compression process, which is reversible, ONR leads to a permanent decline in entropy within the system, resulting in a considerable fraction of ONR compared to the standard value. By meticulously manipulating the parameters of a quantum dimer model, our experiment verifies that the optical compression method can indeed produce a substantial amount of ONR. Furthermore, our findings pave the way for a more efficient and practical method of energy production. Ultimately, our investigation into ONR fosters a deeper understanding of the global instability in thermodynamics and fosters innovative improvements to energy conversion technologies. The experimental results are corroborated through simultaneous simulations. It is anticipated that the experimental outcomes presented here will facilitate future quantum experiments focusing on the themes of irreversibility, fractional work, and efficient compression. We propose a set of theoretical challenges inspired by the Fenton minimax problem, where we aim to find the degree $k$ of a polynomial on the interval $[-1,1]$ that has the minimum value when a specific expression involving $k$ is minimized. Similar challenges are considered for the sum of translates functions. Minimax problems with Chebychev weight have the additional goal of determining the degree $k$ and nodes $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ that minimize the expression $\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|p(x)-Q_n(x)|$, where $p$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ and $Q_n$ is a quadratic polynomial involving the values of $p$ at $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. It is known that we can achieve an error bound of order $\frac{1}{n^{1/2}}$ with $n$ nodes, and our theoretical challenge is to prove that this is the best possible order up to a logarithmic factor. Furthermore, we consider a version of the Fenton challenge for the sum of translates functions, where we aim to translate functions $p_{j}(x)=p(x-e_{j})$ and seek the translation vector $e$ minimizing the expression $\sum_{j=1}^{n}|p(x)-p_{j}(x)|$ at specified nodes. This paper presents an innovative approach to blind image restoration, a family of problems that encompass related tasks such as blind deblurring, super-resolution, and blind de-noising, the common goal being to amplify the clarity of a damaged image by restoring its intensity and sparsity within a given frame size. We delve into these problems by extracting relevant information from the Fourier transform of the image without any additional references, the approach involving extracting sparsity in the form of localized data within a specified radius. We utilize the kernel mixture model to represent this localized data, demonstrating that the dimensions of a kernel representation are sufficient for extracting key features of localized data. This insight enables us to develop a universal solution framework for blind image restoration, the effectiveness of which is demonstrated through successful applications in blind deblurring and super-resolution. It's proven that any solution to the nuybe can be viewed as a weighted sum (or more specifically, a finite combination of complex weights) of solutions to the ybe. Furthermore, we explore various categorical aspects related to the nuybe, including the instances of uniqueness for up to isomorphism nuybe solutions, the extension of these solutions to the nuybe through convolution, and the Upmeier-Lenard-Snider theorem. Examples of nuybe solutions are given based on the twisted nilpotent Yang-Baxter equation and the algebraic torus. It's also shown that the inverse of an nuybe solution, defined as its 'conjugate', exists under specific algebraic and associative conditions and that the nuybe solution's conjugate can be obtained directly from its twisted form. Lastly, we give conditions under which the nuybe solution's conjugate corresponds to an ybe solution. Additionally, we provide the rigorous proof of a property related to the nuybe solution's convolution, which was previously given heuristically in another study. Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and atomic force microscopy, specifically examining the viscoelastic response of lipid raft model membranes comprised of dioleoyl-phosphatidylcholine (DOPC) and varying amounts of dioleoyl-phosphatidylethanol (DOPE) with or without cholesterol, revealed notable discrepancies between the measured bending moduli and expected values for a homogeneous membrane. Furthermore, data indicates that the presence of cholesterol leads to a significant decrease in the bending modulus, with results essentially unchanged when DOPE replaces dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylcholine (DPPC) in the membrane. Analysis of these findings, combined with existing data for DOPC membranes containing increasing amounts of palmitoyl-12-sulforyl phosphatidylglycerol (PSG), suggests a critical relationship between the glycerol moiety and raft-scale membrane stiffness within a certain temperature range, effectively demonstrating how rafts form under physiological conditions. Moreover, data reveals that the observed stiffness enhancements attributed to cholesterol are largely illusory, arising from the increased presence of exchangeable spin labeled phospholipids in the membrane. Ultimately, this research emphasizes the importance of assessing membrane structure through multiple experimental and theoretical methods. While certain techniques may not directly uncover membrane composition, they can provide crucial insights that are essential for developing effective models of membrane-membrane interactions. By recognizing the limitations of specific experimental and theoretical methods, scientists can avoid misinterpreting certain membrane states, such as raft formation, and thereby develop a more comprehensive understanding of membrane-lipid relationships. By combining data from various approaches, including curvature induced unbinding forces and nanomechanical properties, researchers can establish a more accurate model of the membrane, its molecular structure and stiffness. Furthermore, this research highlights how the unique stiffness of PSG lipids, regardless of whether they are in an ordered or disordered membrane phase, plays a significant role in forming stable cholesterol-induced rafts within a wide range of temperatures. Therefore, this research encourages a critical assessment of existing membrane models and suggests new membrane structures that are consistent with a wide variety of experimental measurements. In ordered rewriting systems with a disharmony indicator, we focus on its specific subset, called Gray classes. Each Gray class contains a unique element, known as the Gray quote, which is obtained by applying a rewriting process to the system's initial elements. The notion of Gray reducibility is then defined based on this quote, with a specific class being fully self-consistent if no element is reducable to another within that class. The equilibrium point represents a state where no element is reducible to another. Consistency is also considered, where no element can be rewritten into another within that class. Notably, Sivak-Clarke's 2016 equilibrium characterization fails when applied to rewriting processes in Gray classes. The authors then provide alternatives to this theorem, specifically for Sivak-Clarke's 2016 equilibrium characterization and the related notion of consistency. The study draws parallels between a specific type of rewriting system, known as the Fibonacci system, and a mathematical concept, known as high-dimensional formal power series. The Fibonacci system's equilibrium and consistency were already established through another form of characterization in a 2019 study. The authors also explore a specific type of fully self-consistent class known as a 'finitely reducible class'. They show that no element is reducable to another within that class after a specific number, known as the 'finite reduction threshold', is reached. The authors then provide the equilibrium quote for the Fibonacci system's Gray classes. The study reveals that while the Fibonacci system's equilibrium classes are either finitely reducible or infinitely deep, the general pattern may not always hold for other rewriting processes in Gray classes. The study highlights the need for further research on this type of system, suggesting that no consistent classes may exist, yet the authors also show that fully self-consistent classes do exist. The study draws a parallel between a specific type of rewriting process, known as the Moran system, and a mathematical concept, known as the bivariate generating function. The Moran system's equilibrium and consistency were already established through another form of characterization in a 2017 study. The authors then consider the general case where a system's elements can be rewritten in multiple ways, known as the multi-rewrite general case. The study reveals that while the multi-rewrite general case maintains a number of positive results from previous studies, the equilibrium and consistency characterizations that applied to single-rewrite systems do not generally apply to multi-rewrite systems. The hippocampus, crucial for learning and memory, is exceptionally sensitive to brain scans in Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy.  Diagnosing hippocampal abnormalities in MRI images has the potential to determine a patient's cognitive status and forecast their likelihood of future neurological disorders. Establishing the optimal hippocampal segmentation boundaries poses an image segmentation problem, necessitating the development of an image segmentation framework to define these boundaries. This research proposes a novel hippocampal segmentation framework that uses multiple convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to tackle the right posterior hippocampus segmentation in left anterior hippocampus labeled 3D MRI volumes. This framework comprises three components: a primary CNN module for generating right hippocampi in left hippocampus containing volumes, a parallel CNN module for generating left hippocampi in right hippocampus containing volumes, and a connector CNN module for merging right and left hippocampi. To establish a baseline for our proposed connector strategy, we developed a traditional connector framework using a single CNN. To evaluate our proposed framework and methods, we conducted a cross-database test, demonstrating that our proposed framework achieved a mean dice coefficient of 0.3445, outperforming the traditional framework with a dice value of 0.2666. This research was based on the AutoHippCampSeg Database which contains 401 left hippocampus containing volumes and 401 right hippocampus containing volumes. Each hippocampus containing volume has an annotated portion of its left or right hippocampus. This research was carried out in accordance with the CRUCEXL protocol to enhance the accuracy of its image labels. In addition to its image database contribution, this research developed a proposed framework with a higher dice coefficient and fewer false regions than a traditional framework. This framework was also based on a smaller dataset than other CNN studies. This research is a continuation of our other hippocampus containing framework studies, specifically HippocampSeg. Our study explores how an entangled quantum state, represented by a specific set of vectors, evolves when an additional non-entangled state is introduced, focusing on a particular type of three-mode state called the transversal N-mode state (TNM). To achieve this, we examine the one- and two-particle correlation functions of states constructed by combining TNMs with single-photon states (TPNs). Our analysis shows that as the number of modes (N) tends towards infinity, certain correlation functions exhibit a pigeonhole-like behavior, where a collection of functions with many distinct values converges towards a set value. We observe that for TPNs, this pigeonhole behavior can arise even when only a small number of modes (N = 3) and can be experimentally observed with current technologies. Our findings also reveal a connection between the statistical alignment of direction and the long-term correlations within a system, where the former correlates with higher order but not necessarily lower order correlations. Moreover, this phenomenon serves as a distinct indicator of entanglement, different from measures like the von Neumann entropy, which correlates with lower order correlations. As such, our study contributes to the understanding of how entanglement manifests in a quantum system, where measurements of lower order correlations provide entropy, while measurements of higher order correlations provides alignment. Both types of correlations are essential for different tasks, and our findings experimentally demonstrate the concept with very low order correlations. Our experiment also points to future tasks that could benefit from this phenomenon. One possibility could be to use it for the purposes of quantum metrology by entangling a state with a known reference state to boost measurements, or alternatively, to use it to enhance the capability of a system to resist disturbances through a similar process. Our study experimentally points to these possibilities and suggests several indicators to monitor the phenomenon in future experiments. One suggestion is to use the concept's connection to the Mandel Q-parameter, where the pigeonhole effect can arise when the parameter is close to one, either because the quantum system has only two modes or because a three-mode mode has been entangled with a single-photon mode. Our study concludes by applying these suggestions to the concepts of quantum metrology and resistance to disturbances, which could benefit from this phenomenon. Furthermore, we also examine the influence of the node reconnection strategy on convergence speed. As a result, we hope the framework can serve as a powerful reference for researchers working with graph-structured data and help the community to achieve faster convergence speeds. Our model, based on the 'complex mix' model, is reworked to account for the distinct behaviors of larger grains, PAHs, and the effects of snow lines, showing promise in accurately representing dust properties in the sparse interstellar medium. This research proposes a novel technique in Abstract Interpretation that determines a precision level mid-way through a reachability analysis, suitable for real-time systems. We introduce a new class of precision definitions that rise quickly at analysis commencement, peak at mid-analysis, and gradually decrease until analysis completion. This new precision class is based on'markedness,' a property first identified in Basic Abstract Interpretation. We develop a method to determine the optimal'marking' level for reaching a system's halting state at mid-analysis, resulting in an improved final precision. This improvement is in terms of both set-based and metric-based precision, as proven through theoretical analysis. An experimental evaluation was conducted on a variety of non-trivial linear systems. Compared to standard Reachability Analysis, the resulting computation time was substantially reduced - an average 200 times less, with some cases requiring only 10% of the original time, on an average of a 500-time increase in analysis time to reach the halting state. We have created a tool called decoupling, based on this proposed technique, available at the specified URL. This tool allows for customizable analysis parameters such as the level of advancement in analysis, the degree of 'dilution' of states, and the precision of results. Additionally, we have conducted a parameter optimization technique for finding optimal parameters for a given system's analysis. We have tested the tool on various timing-based systems, all of which yielded parameter sets resulting in precise analysis results. Finally, we have discussed how to adapt this technique to other Advanced Applications of Abstract Interpretation. The technique is expected to find other useful precision definitions that rise and fall during analysis. For instance, one such definition was already discovered - 'dominance,' a known property. We have tested 'dominance' in conjunction with'markedness' on a small, but growing set of systems. Results indicate that 'dominance' can yield precise analysis results, although a more thorough experimental evaluation is required to fully understand its behavior. Domination is a property that enforces a partial ordering, thus it may be a useful precision definition for systems exhibiting non-interrupting task behaviors, such as web sites. Moreover, given a system's correct implementation, the system's code is guaranteed to satisfy 'dominance,' making it a useful technique for developers looking to enforce their own precision definitions. In summary, a new technique has been proposed that is expected to find other useful precision definitions to describe the behavior of concurrent systems reliably and efficiently. The results show that the absence of inversion symmetry in bulk SrTiO3 is not a prerequisite for topological phonons to occur. Instead, these phonons are influenced by the orbital symmetry breaking caused by photoexcitation, which also results in a large phonon gap. The topological phonon gap diminishes as the orbital symmetry breaking decreases. The presence of topological phonons is linked to a new light-regulated phonon state near the Dirac point, which we refer to as an "phononic Dirac loop". This state might be observable through Sr isotope nuclear recoil scattering experiments. The representation learning approach with community awareness has become increasingly prominent in graph embedding, yet its state corresponds to early advancements that depend on predefined community structures. In response, this paper proposes a novel fairness-focused representation learning strategy, named $\textit{LocalCFA}$, with the aim of addressing the constraints associated with predefined community structures. $\textit{LocalCFA}$ represents a hierarchical fair sharing framework composed of a central node, its neighbors, and their immediate surroundings. It proposes a comprehensive theoretical framework to capture Local Community Fairness and leverages this concept to design an effective objective function. Further, $\textit{LocalCFA}$ is implemented using a combination of autoregressive functions and graph neural networks, achieving improved effectiveness according to experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world data. Beyond its superior performance, $\textit{LocalCFA}$ offers notable advantages in fairness, complexity, and controllability. Ultimately, $\textit{LocalCFA}$ presents a groundbreaking strategy for fair representation learning that goes beyond the conventional group-level approach by promoting local community fairness. It also promotes innovative research avenues in fairness-focused representation learning. The code for $\textit{LocalCFA}$ is available at https://github.com/MITIE-LID/LocalCFA. As a form of contribution to the graph learning community, this paper conducts a systematic evaluation of the effect of community size on the performance of $\textit{LocalCFA}$, revealing a size-sensitive attribute discrimination characteristic. Therefore, this research offers valuable insights into the design of fairness-focused representation learning methods, inspiring the graph learning community to consider the impact of community size on the effectiveness of representation learning models. Lastly, to facilitate the interaction between the community structure and the learning process, this paper proposes a novel strategy, allowing $\textit{LocalCFA}$ to adaptively select community sizes and adapt to their inherent properties, thereby enhancing its effectiveness. The learned representations are available at https://github.com/MITIE-LID/LocalCFA/commits/main. Review-based product recommendation is a crucial task for e-commerce websites, where the ultimate goal is to predict a user's future ratings for a specific product based on their previous reviews and historical interactions. Although advancements have significantly improved prediction accuracy, the field still faces two primary challenges: (1) improving the feasibility of interactive models by minimizing reliance on user input; (2) enhancing the robustness of current models when dealing with noisy or incomplete data. Currently available models are sensitive to user reviews but often rely too heavily on these reviews, neglecting their historical interactions and resulting in poor predictions when user inputs are unavailable. Furthermore, real-world review datasets often contain significant noise, making it challenge for models to distinguish between informative and uninformative reviews. Therefore, our solution, Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), combines the efficiency of non-interactive models and the effectiveness of interactive models, while incorporating robustness against noisy reviews and low reliance on user inputs. By using a sentiment classifier to filter noisy reviews and an attention-based mechanism to prioritize informative reviews, SIFN enhances predicted ratings and recommendation performance. Evaluation results demonstrate that SIFN surpasses state-of-the-art baselines on three public datasets and two benchmark tasks. For efficient partitioning of large hexahedral meshes, high-performance computing (HPC) practitioners rely on pre-defined, user-specified partitioning schemes. These typically involve uniform sectoral divisions but can also incorporate customized segmentations like reflecting and rotating half-cubes. Nonetheless, current methods fall short in addressing segmented meshes resulting from cutting operations within Hexahedral meshes, which are commonly employed in HPC domains. To address this limitation, we propose a method for automatically generating partitioning schemes that incorporate tets resulting from hexahedral mesh cutting. We achieve this by introducing a new type of sector consisting of multiple tets, which allows for increased flexibility in partitioning designs. Furthermore, this method enables the incorporation of reflecting and rotating half-cubes, thereby reducing the total number of sectorial elements required. We demonstrate an extensive evaluation of our approach, which showcases its efficacy by comparing the number of sectorial elements needed to partition a given hexahedral mesh with and without incorporating cutting tetrahedra. Specifically, our approach allows for reducing the number of sectorial elements by a factor of 2 to 58, which substantially decreases the time and effort required to generate partitioning schemes in practice. To showcase the applicability of our approach, we utilized a computation involving cutting simulations on a Boeing Cessna aircraft model, which demonstrated a notable reduction in partitioning complexity. We successfully partitioned the resulting large hexahedral mesh with cutting tetrahedras using a relatively coarse 16^3 sectorial partitioning, which yielded results concordant to those obtained using finer 40^3 sectorial partitioning designed without cutting tets. We implemented the proposed approach using the ifcart HPC tool and publicly released a accompanying Python module titled "cart_py". Furthermore, we released a given cutting simulation dataset "cut_sim_data" on GitHub, which serves as a comprehensive test case for evaluating partitioning schemes. We intend to continuously expand the cut_tet_hex.py module to widely available partitioning schemes. A future extension of this work will involve developing algorithms within the cart_hpc framework to generate partitioning schemes from any mesh, regardless of its topology or origin. Moreover, we will leverage advanced geometric analysis techniques to optimize cutting tetrahedras for efficient partitioning. By promoting efficient partitioning schemes through cart_hpc, we aim to empower HPC practitioners to achieve better outcomes in domains such as cutting simulations and physics-based rendering. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a connection in their fundamental structure, which involves identifying the relationships between entities. This similarity in structure prompts the question of whether there is a two-way relationship between the performance of a model in link prediction and its ability to perform relation extraction. In other words, does improving a model's capacity to accurately predict links between entities in a graph, using auxiliary information, subsequently enable it to more effectively identify the relationships between entities in a sentence? Our investigation reveals that this is indeed the case. Specifically, we demonstrate that fine-tuning a model on a link prediction task improves its performance in relation extraction and this improvement can be further enhanced by leveraging auxiliary information to refine the auxiliary context of the auxiliary sentences in the link prediction task. Experimental results validate our hypothesis, with notable gains in performance observed on the STS-B, CR, and Conrel datasets. The code used in this study is available on GitHub at https://github.com/rgwt/rel-extr-to-lp. One significant challenge in off-policy deep reinforcement learning is dealing with the high dimensionality of the action-value function's action component, which describes a three-dimensional spatial location. In our work, we tackle this issue by introducing a novel action discretization framework that assigns a meaningful, structured set of actions, thereby simplifying the action-space to a manageable size. By representing the action-space as a union of regular, convex, three-dimensional volumes, we address the issue of samples falling outside these boundaries, ensuring that learned policies remain continuous across the discretized space. We develop a theoretical framework for determining the size of these regions such that the resulting policy is continuous with respect to any metric on the action-space. Empirical results validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating that the resulting policy can indeed be continuous, as supported by our experimental findings, which highlight the relationship between the size of these regions and the resulting policy's continuity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that hand-engineered designs, while conceptually analogous to our approach, fail to meet their intended goal of promoting continuity in the policy. Finally, we show that our approach can be applied to a variety of task scenarios, such as dynamic environments and multi-agent systems. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dkopecký/coarse-grained-continuity. 

Key Contributions:

1. A novel coarsely-grained action discretization framework that assigns actions to structured, three-dimensional volumes, enabling a more manageable and coherent action-space.
2. A novel coarse-grained Q-function framework that assigns three-dimensional volumes to actions, allowing a more manageable and coherent action-space.
3. A theoretical framework for determining the size of these regions such that the resulting policy can be continuous.
4. Experimental results demonstrating that these regions can effectively guarantee the continuity of the resulting policy.
5: A proposed approach to determining the size of these regions, as well as a proposed metric for measuring continuity in the policy.

Moreover, the method is efficient, computationally cost-effective, and capable of handling large-scale simulations. Current models of social learning in robots often rely on variational inference-based representations and intrinsic motivation to effectively interact with humans in complex tasks.  This research indicates that robots adapt better and require less adjustment when using transfer empowerment, a motivation mechanism that empowers robots to be more adaptable to different situations.  However, existing versions of transfer empowerment are non-deterministic, which makes them unreliable in real-world applications.  We propose a new, verifiable version of transfer empowerment that provides an accurate measure of a robot's behavior within a predetermined range.  This is achieved through a probabilistic conversion of the policy to a Deterministic Finite State Machine.  We demonstrate that our approach enhances the predictability of transfer empowerment, yielding a notable improvement in a social learning experiment.  This result is validated by both human-generated trajectories, taught by human instructors, as well as self-directed learning through imitation.  Notably, our study also explores the influence of social learning scenarios on the properties of generated models and evaluates their applicability through a comparison with existing, non-deterministic methods of transfer empowerment.  We further highlight potential benefits and limitations of our approach and provide guidance on its implementation for future research purposes. We introduce a novel method for matching local features without a detector, in a category-level retrieval context, by directly comparing the spatial relationships of points within a query image to those in a dataset of candidates. Our approach, LoFTR, utilizes self- and cross-attention mechanisms to identify corresponding areas and calculates a category-level score based on spatial coherence across all categories and the query image. Unlike traditional deep learning-based retrieval methods, LoFTR does not require pre-trained detectors to extract local features, leveraging the stability of the transformation of local points instead. This allows our method to run significantly faster, be relatively lightweight, and robust to poor illumination and noise. We demonstrate LoFTR's efficacy on the FLIR dataset and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of LoFTR under uniform illumination conditions and highlight its ability to effectively localize objects of minimal length, such as handgun grips. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com Research com/LoFTR. Our method won the Utility Track first prize in NeurIPS 2021. Compressing large neural networks by reducing their parameters or dimensions has been successful, but there's a less explored side to this process - compressing the model itself by limiting the complexity of its internal structures. From simplified component representations to condensed representation of the model's parameters, various methods can effectively reduce compression costs. Notably, representing the model as a sequence of decision trees with a limited number of branches can be particularly efficient. Nonetheless, implementing such a compression directly from existing models is complicated due to its lack of correspondence to the model's decision-making processes. Therefore, we explore a new perspective on model compression - learning a simplified model representation while maintaining its predictive capabilities - in this study. We adapted a range of machine learning problems, including binary classification and 1-D regression, to several compression types including decision tree, k-mean, and binary dimension compression. We also introduced new compression methods, such as learning a binary function and low-weight pruning, which often yielded better results and enabled us, for the first time, to compress large models directly. Our findings reveal that some compression methods are more effective than others and that their success depends on the type of model architecture. Additionally, compressing a model reduces both training and testing times, but the actual speedup depends on the specific compression method and model architecture. We also observed that some features are more relevant than others in contributing to the model's performance, and that time-based low-weight pruning can effectively eliminate unnecessary model parameters while maintaining predictive capabilities. We developed an innovative new compression method, participant dropout, which participates in actual training processes, is not biased and benefits from being used in small portions. We also obtained results indicating that participating in training in a small way has a positive effect on test accuracy, and that such effect can be attributed to a reduced impact of regularization, and more trained parameters have a positive effect on test accuracy, and that such effect can be attributed to incorporating knowledge from trained parameters in training. We complemented our study with an evaluation of several potential methods for evaluating compressed models, and found that one such method, decompressing the model and evaluating its components - known as backtracking - effectively evaluates a model's capabilities and predicts its performance in different compression scenarios and models. Ultimately, we obtained results indicating that given enough resources, it's possible to effectively reduce a model's complexity while maintaining its predictive capabilities and reducing training and testing times. The developed methods for achieving this goal can effectively compress a range of neural network models for use in different applications. We examine the properties of the empirical distribution of equilibrium states within disjoint subsets of the continuous spectrum of a Feller diffusion. It's discovered that this distribution possesses a unique sampling distribution, which aligns with the standard central limit theorem, where'standard' can be achieved through a combination of the diffusion processes in question. Furthermore, this sampling distribution is insensitive to the structural details of the specified subspaces, thereby yielding a quantity that can be calculated efficiently, especially for a wide variety of subspaces. Consequently, this calculated distribution is proposed as an estimator for the equilibrium state density of a Feller diffusion, which helps address a longstanding issue first brought up by Donsker and Kertz (1984) regarding the fact that equilibrium states are not part of the weak limit of equilibrium distributions in a system experiencing an increasing period of time. Our method of combination and sampling distributions for disjoint subspaces can be extended and broadened to subspaces that overlap with one another. It's noted that subspaces sharing a common component, albeit faint or distant, have a heightened likelihood of encountering convergence, particularly in regards to a unique sampling distribution, which in turn aids in the identification of spectral shifts. Examples are presented to illustrate and validate the theoretical concepts at hand. To handle the challenges posed by hierarchical data, we develop FGNET-RH, a novel neural architecture that leverages Poincar\'{e} hyperbolic space geometry and graph structure for named entity recognition, taking advantage of inherent tree-based relationships in semantic information to speed up training and efficiency. FGNET-RH achieves this through its refined multi-scale representations of tree structures in hyperbolic space, which are learned end-to-end, and its integration of soft F1-metric loss for regulating negative predictions. By adapting efficient GraphSAGE's multi-scale neighbor aggregation and convolution layers to hyperbolic space, FGNET-RH provides a scalable framework that can accommodate complex tree structures without requiring explicit graph reconstruction. Our experiments show FGNET-RH achieves superior performance on benchmark datasets such as CoNLL-2003, TAC KBP, and NILVDO (including NYU, MIT, and Harvard), surpassing state-of-the-art results including linear models with CNN and Char Embeddings, BERT-BERT-Path-Encoder, and PNet-Edge RGNet models. Furthermore, FGNET-RH demonstrates substantial gains in training efficiency, requiring less data (1/3 to 1/9) and reducing computation time to transfer Poincar\'{e} hyperbolic space embeddings for KBP annual datasets from O(n^2) to O(n^1.2). FGNET-RH's ability to efficiently utilize hierarchical data relationships makes it well-suited for knowledge graph-based natural language processing applications. FGNET-RH's code will be publicly available.

This study explores the concept of causal effects (CE) between two sets of data, developing on existing frameworks such as (1) the orthogonal CE for orthogonal data sets, and (2) the reduced CE for non-orthogonal data sets as defined by Kockelberg et al. (2021). We identify two inaccuracies in these frameworks: a flaw in part (1) - the over estimation of CE, and a limitation in part (2) - the need for knowledge of data dimensions. We correct these issues by developing a new definition for non-orthogonal data CE, under the umbrella of joint probability mass function (JPMF) and revealing that this new definition offers the tightest possible CE bounds. Additionally, our method has an almost linear computational complexity, making it suitable for high-dimensional data analysis. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach through two real world applications - the estimation of semantic-related CE for word vectors and the estimation of causal effects of advertising campaigns on sales, utilizing available data. Our estimation results for both scenarios consistently provide tighter CE bounds compared to established, highly optimized tools. We corroborate these findings with analysis drawn from information theory and the notion of causality. Our method has been made available under an open-source license at https://github.com/EdouardLefevbre/jpmf_cae. (i) For knowledge to have an impact, it must be correlated with something it doesn't cause. In practice, this translates to knowing the probability distribution of two sets of data being jointly dependent. This is an extremely general condition, and our new definition of CE offers a straightforward and efficient means of addressing this challenge. (ii) Granger causality, as defined by Clare and Knight (2004-2005), represents an efficient and highly scalable means of estimating CE under specific, real-world assumptions. Our approach offers the added benefit of resilience to these assumptions. (iii) Our definition of CE and associated bounds can be used to estimate multidimensional causes, thereby offering a means of evaluating and explaining the practicality of our approach in this context. Our work showcases the effectiveness of our CE definition and associated bounds in real-world applications through the estimation of word vector semantic-related CE and advertising campaign causal effects. The analysis also considers the efficacy of reward networks and ensemble learning in fine-tuning the model under monitored and unmonitored conditions. The summary generation results obtained from GAE-ISumm outperformed reference models in terms of metrics such as ROUGE, with notable gains in ensemble-based and reward network-driven summaries. Most current methods for analyzing temporal actions rely on substantial amounts of labeled data, particularly the fine-grained segmental labels, making them unsuitable for many practical scenarios requiring high accuracy. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel unsupervised approach known as Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP), capable of discovering high-quality segmental labels from limited fine-grained labels. SS CAP incorporates a rare action model that detects co-occurring actions and their time frames, a parser that infers more complex actions from simpler ones, and a model optimizing mechanism to ensure the learned results align with the given labels. On top of this, we establish a new dataset with expert annotations, called NUSSEG, specifically aimed at expert annotations, to validate the efficacy of SS CAP. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, SS CAP yields a substantial improvement of 9.5mAP% on UCF101-24, 6.2mAP% on GTEA, and 4.1mAP% on NUSSEG. Furthermore, in experiments on NUSSEG, SS CAP outperforms paragraph-level baselines with significant gains of 14mAP% on segmental recognition and 10mAP% on overall mAP, demonstrating its robust performance. The proposed method effectively discovers fine-grained segmental labels from limited labels and rare actions, thereby eliminating the need for expensive manual labor. While SS CAP shares some components with semi-supervised models, it distinctively parses activities without relying on additional labels. Ultimately, SS CAP achieves superior performance compared to unsupervised and semi-supervised models on two public datasets and its proposed NUSSEG dataset, showcasing its robustness across various settings. The conventional approach to assessing student programming abilities in academic settings has been the subject of empirical studies. These studies aim to address a fundamental question: Are the standard evaluation methods effective in predicting student programming capabilities, or do they often fall short? This study builds on previous research by focusing on testing and debugging skills, which are viewed as critical components of the typical programming assessment process. To this end, the educational platform, Autograder, was used to evaluate the performance of 342 students enrolled in a university course. Students were divided into two groups for assessment: one that provided detailed feedback on their code, and another that received only conceptual information. Each group was evaluated based on two criteria: the students' programming skills and their understanding of the assessment concepts. The results showed a notable disparity in the performance of the two groups, with the students receiving conceptual feedback exhibiting a significantly higher score. Furthermore, the study found a positive correlation between the students' programming and conceptual assessment scores, indicating that providing detailed feedback does not enhance a student's performance. The study's findings provide valuable insights for educators, suggesting that incorporating an additional assessment method that focuses on conceptual understanding can be an effective strategy to improve student performance. This method can be implemented in a typical assessment environment by assigning two separate tasks: one requiring students to explain their code, and another where the code is provided without explanation. These resources are available under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. Specifically, the dataset and video recordings for this study can be accessed at the designated links. In addition to this investigation, the study contributes to the body of research by proposing a set of empirical key performance indicators, the effect of prior knowledge, the classification of conceptual and procedural knowledge, the dynamics of the assessment process, and the potential of the Autograder platform as a testing ground for future educational research. A novel deep learning approach has been developed to improve such tasks, building on previous successes in related fields and incorporating performance metrics that take into account the actual data collected, or "labels." The architecture's design is motivated by understanding its ability to learn patterns within the data, and its effectiveness is illustrated through its application in utilizing the data to locate cosmic rays' interactions within sensitive detector arrays. The approach yields superior results when trained on simulated data of COSMIC RAYS, outperforming a more basic method that relies on pattern recognition, and demonstrating its potential to adapt to various data configurations by successfully localizing events on the Frejus detector, a real-world device. The architecture's flexibility and ability to handle diverse data scenarios make it a valuable asset for astroparticle researchers and potential applications in related fields. The approach yields superior results when trained on thickness-reconstructed data of both PMTs, outperforming a more basic method that relies on pattern recognition. In this context, the theories involving states, operators, and processes from a specific C*-algebra are reinterpreted as instances of a larger pre-functoral framework, while the theory involving generalized measurements is seen as an exception. Furthermore, the theories involving states and operators can also be viewed as instances of a larger categorical framework. We analyze long-term, non-stationary time series that are subject to various forms of heavy-tailed noise, such as ARMA heavy-tail noise and 1/f heavy-tail noise. We begin by providing a precise definition of a class of statistics called depth-based statistics, which capture the behavior of such time series. We develop novel, strong consistency results for this class of statistics, building on earlier work by trying to apply existing methods from multivariate heavy-tail theory but finding them inadequate for our specific case. Instead, we had to establish a precision theorem for the quantity in question, which involves a complex combination of the properties of heavy-tail probability and Pafumi's regenerative function technique. This allows us to infer that our depth-based statistics converge to a specific mean, which in turn enables us to make a range of conclusions about the convergence of the statistics. We draw insights from our findings by considering a concrete example of a heavy-tailed time series inspired by neuroscience. Our analysis reveals some surprising and subtle correlations between the parameters of the time series, which highlights the need for careful estimation in order to make reliable inferences. We further explore the ability to estimate the parameters of the time series using our convergence results, showing that simple and robust techniques can be effective, but that the best technique to use depends on the specific characteristics of the time series. Finally, we end by considering the various limitations of our findings and how they could be addressed in future research. The main conclusions can be summarized as follows: (i) in the case of ARMA heavy-tail noise, we have a simple and elegant conclusion that our depth-based statistics converge to a specific mean; (ii) in the case of 1/f heavy-tail noise, we have a less optimal conclusion due to a lower order of convergence; (iii) both cases are suboptimal in comparison to the results obtained for univariate heavy-tail time series; (iv) the convergence results rely on a precise definition of heavy-tail probability and regenerative function techniques. Therefore, a natural open problem arises: what happens if we consider the case of multivariate heavy-tail noise? Our analysis reveals some surprising correlations between the parameters of the time series, which suggests a natural future research direction: investigate the properties of multivariate heavy-tail noise. The proposed research aims to explore these questions and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the behavior of heavy-tail noise in multivariate time series. Despite numerous advantages of sequential data in characterizing dynamic phenomena, time series learning often poses significant difficulties. The complexities stem from the temporal dependencies, non-uniform sampling, high dimensionality, noisy nature, irregular structures, and the need for representations that effectively reflect temporal sequences, making it a particularly challenging task in the life sciences where predictions are crucial. To address this, we propose the Guided Neural Network for temporal data (GNNt), a lightweight yet efficient architecture that integrates external knowledge to facilitate learning in networks with temporal data. The proposed method leverages the benefits of graph-based models, incorporating temporal dependencies and high-dimensional information into a single, unified framework. The proposed method is evaluated on two prominent problems in the life sciences: predicting continuous biological processes, such as protein-protein interactions, and analyzing cyclic behaviors over extended periods, such as menstrual cycle assessments. The results demonstrate that GNNt outperforms existing methods, achieving remarkable performance with a mere 10% of available data. The study's code and pre-trained models are freely available for use. With the proposed method, the life sciences can now efficiently learn from temporal data, leading to a significant paradigm shift in how high-dimensional temporal data is perceived and processed. The research also highlights the importance of interpreting neural network predictions in the life sciences to gain a deeper understanding of how these models operate. The study's outcomes have significant implications for a wide array of scientific and medical predictive challenges. The analysis and demonstration of how temporal data can be represented are discussed in the context of their applications. The research encourages the integration of high-dimensional temporal data representation learning as a primary objective in the life sciences, thus paving the way for a more streamlined and scientific approach to developing supervised learning algorithms in the field. Recurrent neural networks are capable of modeling intricate tasks that involve sequential decision-making in complex environments. One key feature of such tasks is often the existence of hidden states, which contain essential yet inaccessible information to the decision-maker. We explore a specific category of task called partially-observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in which the decision-maker has limited insight into the hidden state of the environment. Previous studies on POMDPs rely heavily on the use of entropy-based methods to mitigate the impact of incomplete information, but our research reveals that neural networks can learn to adapt to the specific structure of POMDP tasks, even when the hidden states concern the decision-maker's beliefs. Consequently, we raise the question of how the inner workings of recurrent neural networks, which have demonstrated outstanding capability in tackling POMDP tasks, relate to entropy-based methods used in theoretical POMDP studies. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the hidden patterns within POMDP tasks that are solved by neural networks, which has practical implications for the optimization of entropy-based methods. Furthermore, as many applications of POMDPs involve the assessment of risk, our findings suggest a new method to improve the detection of relevant features when utilizing neural networks in such contexts. One potential application of our discoveries is to the field of asset management by enabling better diagnosis of the hidden states of system health in partially-observable maintenance environments. Finally, through our analysis of a real-world dataset from the Time Series Prediction Competition, we demonstrate the feasibility of applying POMDP concepts to practical challenges beyond asset management. Overall, our study sheds light on the interplay between theoretical POMDP studies and the practical capabilities of recurrent neural networks. As our analysis indicates, neural networks can learn to effectively mitigate the impact of incomplete information by adapting to the specific structure of POMDP tasks. Consequently, by improving our understanding of this adaptation, we may enhance the optimization of entropy-based methods, which have significant theoretical implications for a broader range of learning tasks. Furthermore, as our research reveals, analyzing the inner workings of neural networks, which have demonstrated outstanding capability in tackling POMDP tasks, can provide practical insights for the optimization of entropy-based methods. Finally, as our findings suggest, POMDP concepts can be effectively applied to tackling real-world challenges that involve variable information availability. Recent advancements in federated learning have led to rapid progress in training machine learning models using a vast array of devices. Nevertheless, the current state of communication-intensive FL, which involves frequent model gradient updates, significantly hampers performance due to suboptimal convergence and prolonged training periods. To counter this challenge, our proposed approach, DP-REC, combines reliable statistical metrics with a biased, yet efficient neural network model approximation to achieve rapid convergence while maintaining data privacy and resilience against adverse client data. DP-REC accomplishes this by means of a distorted neural network model approximation utilizing optical depth metrics, which enables rapid convergence and robust model generalization. Moreover, we introduce an efficient training mechanism that mitigates communication overhead through local optimization, thus substantially decreasing the frequency of required communications. In accordance with the requirements of data privacy, our model is fitted locally, and the parameter updates are synchronized with the central server through asymmetrical communication. In experimental trials, DP-REC has demonstrated substantial gains in model efficiency and convergence rate over existing neural network model approximations such as NeuralDIP and OPT-DIP, while also providing enhanced data privacy protections as specified by the Genomic Privacy Metric. Notably, DP-REC's communication efficiency allows it to achieve a 99.7% reduction in communication bandwidth compared to conventional FL methods for similar model efficiency and convergence rates. The code for DP-REC is publicly available at: https://github.com/himanshusharma42/DP-REC-FedAvg.

The goal was to identify the impact of the interstellar medium's far-ultraviolet continuum on the distribution of young stars within the complex, specifically those associated with filamentary structures. By applying a novel method to deconvolve adjacent bright spots, a smooth far-ultraviolet continuum was obtained that revealed large-scale patterns. Two primary types of patterns were observed: a network of narrow, far-ultraviolet bands along filaments that align with those detected in polarized light through the far-ultraviolet, and broader, diffuse patterns beyond the filaments that show no obvious alignment with star formation regions. By analyzing the distribution of young stars within the complex and their association with these patterns, it was found that they often align with the same filaments as the far-ultraviolet bands, and there's a notable lack of stars within areas characterized by the broader, diffuse patterns, even when these areas are dominated by young stars. By quantifying the density of young stars within the complex and their association with these patterns, it was found that they tend to be less dense in areas with the broader, diffuse patterns and a higher density in areas with the band-like patterns. By correlating these findings at a larger scale, it was discovered that areas with the broader, diffuse patterns tend to be more distant, whereas those with the band-like patterns and denser young stars are more closely linked to cloud cores containing high-mass stars and polarized far-ultraviolet light. Overall, these findings suggest a role for the far-ultraviolet background radiation in setting the overall distribution of young stars within the complex. Furthermore, by leveraging the far-ultraviolet properties of the interstellar medium, it's possible to pinpoint the most distant cloud regions, plan effective observations, and gain insight into the complex dynamics. Specifically regarding the unique system of filaments, it's observed that the observed morphology can be traced back to a combination of a hierarchical collapse and a influence of a nearby supernova/explosion, a million years ago. However, the proposed scenario still faces ongoing investigation and analysis. Meanwhile, regarding the larger Taurus-Auriga-Persius complex, it's noticed that areas with the broader, diffuse patterns appear to be transitioning towards these denser, star-forming conditions. This work investigates multi-phase games with incomplete information. We focus on situations where players can't fully grasp the game's parameters, yet can infer them through sequential stages. Our first goal is to identify the lesser information that would be sufficient for optimal play in each phase. We examine the effectiveness of two methods for determining this 'lesser information'. Firstly, we consider cumulative frequentism, which is based on Bayesian learning. Our results show that this approach leads to optimal play when there is at least a certain level of signal strength. We also clarify under which conditions this experience-based strategy aligns with the minimal necessary information. Secondly, we explore the consistency of two distinct concepts of 'perfect information'. These are the idea of conditional independence between phases and a more general notion of separability. Our results show that when the game's parameters can be broken down into distinct parts, the'separability' condition can be met even when the 'conditional independence' requirement is not. Conversely, we also demonstrate scenarios where these two concepts differ. Furthermore, we establish specific criteria under which the minimal necessary information can be characterised as either conditional independence or separability. These findings have significant implications for understanding the relationships between these concepts in larger contexts. In addition to these theoretical contributions, we also studied the practical application of these concepts to finding the optimal strategy in three types of multi-phase games - binary choice, matching, and auction. Specifically, we considered how these strategies are affected when the game's parameters gradually shift from one phase to another. Our analysis showed that while there is often no single strategy that works for all phases, the optimal strategy for each phase can provide valuable insights and guidance on how to play in other phases. This is especially so in matches, where our results show that the optimal strategy in one phase can provide complete information for the next phase. Finally, we also initiated research on how to determine the minimal necessary information for games with an unlimited number of phases. By adopting a dynamical systems perspective, we can describe how the game's parameters evolve over time and investigate under what conditions they eventually come to rest in a singular point. However, our results also show that in many situations, these evolving dynamics may remain in perpetual motion on intricate geometric shapes, raising important questions for further investigation. These findings suggest that even in situations where the game's dynamics may not ultimately converge, the optimal strategy for each phase can still provide valuable practical guidance and insight. Launched in a custom-made environment mimicking launch conditions, our research focuses on the multi-phase interaction between fluids and rigid structures. Particles driving the system's dynamics through an adapted Gullinou algorithm handle the fluid, while a modified formulation for interactions involving multiple fluids and rigid bodies is developed to replicate physics such as fluid compression, surface tension, and collision resistance. Rigid body simulations utilize a novel Volume Fraction-based method to facilitate flexible contact modeling and efficient energy transfer between fluids and structures. To address limitations of surface tension on the surface of cohesive fluids, a novel ALE-based rippling model is developed. A new generation of quantum machines is being developed to break the algorithmic limitations of classical systems. Despite this, a fundamental problem with learning algorithms remains: how can a quantum system effectively generalize from its findings without constant supervision? We designed an experimental framework that allows a quantum computer to improve its performance autonomously, using a reward system that approximates supervision. Our approach demonstrates that a probability distribution shift can occur without explicit monitoring of the learning process. Additionally, our research team developed an efficient method for reusing educational samples on Anthem, a QAOA processor. Our results demonstrate that a modified QAOA algorithm, when applied to randomized instances of the Max 2 Sat problem, achieves a 22% higher expected solution value compared to the standard QAOA algorithm and a 57% higher expected solution value compared to the vanilla Variational Quantum Eigensolver. Our findings also illustrate the potential of the reformulated VQE algorithm to surpass its classical and quantum precursors. We hypothesize that a similar competitive dynamic could arise in a variety of quantum research platforms and that a particular variation of the quantum evolutionary algorithm may dominate both classical and quantum systems. Our study's experimental findings validate a theoretical model for unmonitored learning, which yields a series of useful results,, including a upper limit on how quickly a distributional shift can occur. Our work's experimental findings were accompanied by a associated code.
