Generating natural-sounding text in dialogue is an intricate task that requires a deep understanding of language use and its underlying patterns and structures. Previous efforts in this area have made significant breakthroughs, yet the underlying organizational frameworks used in research are often not adaptable or collaborative, hindering further progress. This paper proposes a new framework called LEATHER, designed to enhance collaboration among researchers. It offers a systematic approach to analyzing and studying dialogue text, one that is informed by linguistic insights. By building upon existing frameworks, LEATHER provides a flexible structure for generating text in dialogue, supporting various generating methods. Using LEATHER, we have developed multiple natural language production models, all performing within the average range when evaluated using the standard metrics. Our results suggest that, while these models can produce reasonable results, they are not able to capture the complexities of human language, demonstrating the limitations of current approaches. Ultimately, we believe that developing a greater understanding of these complexities requires a more fundamental transformation in NLP research, decoupling it from its current reliance on analysis-by-keyword. Instead, we suggest adopting an analysis-by-structure methodology, one that treats the internal organization of utterances as the primary focus of investigation. By doing so, we may uncover new insights that can ultimately lead to more innovative NLP solutions. A specific machine learning technique known as Chain Gaussian Process (CGP), which combines the concepts of time series and Gaussian Process regression, is proposed in this study to predict and analyze the mechanical stress patterns and loading forces of large offshore wind turbines under unpredictable weather conditions. This advanced learning system integrates the power of Gaussian Processes with the efficiency of deterministic machine learning techniques, which can handle the complex interactions between variables with greater ease. To demonstrate its effectiveness, a large-scale simulation of an S175-6.1 offshore wind turbine was conducted, which took into account the dynamic movements and stress patterns of its blades. To develop the CGP model, a vast database of wind-turbine stress patterns and loading forces was generated using a detailed model based on the Bogdanov hull, which was subject to various severe weather conditions and rotor speeds. By utilizing the CGP method to analyze these complex data sets, which included an array of approximately 500 million non-linear equations and multiple variables, researchers were able to achieve remarkable results. Notably, the models learned using CGP accurately captured the complex interactions and non-linear patterns in the data, which are highly critical in the field of offshore engineering. This includes the accurate simulation of wind-turbine stress patterns and loads under various weather conditions, which has practical implications for offshore engineering and design. Furthermore, the CGP method demonstrated significant potential to reduce the computational complexity of the analysis, which is a crucial consideration in this field. This approach enables the development of finite element models based on Gaussian Processes that can accurately capture non-linear behavior and uncertainty, which can be used to develop complex structures under unpredictable conditions. These models utilize the minimum amount of data necessary for the analysis, which greatly reduces the required computational resources. To conclude, the CGP technique holds great promise in the field of offshore engineering, where it can be utilized to develop complex designs under unpredictable conditions and reduce computational complexity. Moreover, the CGP method and its related open-source tool have significant implications and can facilitate the development of uncertainty-based design methods and simulation models for various engineering applications, which rely heavily on reliability and efficiency. To analyze intricate processes, it's essential to integrate diverse types of data, for example combining X-ray imaging with simulations in a real-time setting. Although there have been significant advancements in incorporating data into simulations, reversing this process and utilizing simulations to inform experimental data is often hindered by the limitations of traditional inverse modeling techniques. These methods struggle to integrate data from multiple sources and are susceptible to the noises present in experimental data, often requiring unrealistic conditions such as perfectly controlled initial values and specific algorithmic combinations. In order to circumvent these problems, we developed an innovative forward-optimization approach that utilizes high-performance simulations to bypass inverse modeling, instead leveraging an intensive strategy of trial-and-error to find the best fit. Utilizing advanced data comparison metrics like time-resolved metrics that assess similarities in multiple data sets, our method searches through a vast parameter space to identify optimal configurations that effectively match simulations with experimental data, including 2D/3D real-time imaging. This approach was successfully tested on a high-pressure diamond cell experiment, specifically studying the high-pressure diamond anvil cell using 2D-fluorescence imaging and 3D-X-ray imaging for the same substances but with different initial conditions. Notably, our results from the pressure-driven cubic phase transition observation using 2D fluorescence imaging and 3D observed diamond dissolution via X-ray imaging revealed that our method could accurately determine pressure and temperature from the 2D data and also pinpoint dissolved regions on the diamond surface. These findings from the 3D X-ray imaging allowed us to verify the consequences of dissolution on the observed cubic phase transition, thereby establishing that our method effectively integrates both types of data into simulations, despite their differing natures and requirements. This study showcases a practical application of our forward-optimization technique to tackle intricate problems, thereby offering a versatile framework for searching through possible configurations to effectively integrate diverse types of data, particularly those requiring different imaging techniques. This paper presents SceNDD, a novel naturalistic driving dataset focusing on common driving situations. The dataset was gathered from a total of 89,629 seconds of driving footage collected from 35 drivers operating a vehicle in everyday conditions, as part of a driving simulation activity. SceNDD encompasses five key categories of driving situations, each encompassing multiple scenarios as defined by the SHHS project. Our work highlights the dataset gathering methodology, evaluation process, and its potential uses, in addition to making the dataset available for public research and development. As an advanced dataset, SceNDD outperforms these alternatives by offering high-quality metrics, intricate driving situation classifications, and a detailed manual evaluation process. Ultimately, SceNDD has the potential to greatly contribute to the advancement of advanced driving assistant systems and serve as a valuable resource for testing and development. Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface-aided communications is growing, with a key component being reliable channel estimation for these systems. Existing proof-of-concept models for channel estimation used deep learning-based techniques like ELM, but these models made unrealistic assumptions about perfect RIS delays. Since practical RIS devices have hardware impairments that affect signal values, we modified the ELM framework by incorporating an extra term into the target function to account for these distortions. Additionally, we adjusted the ELM weights during training, knowing that initial weights would affect early training performance. Our results show that our modified ELM model achieved better performance than the original ELM model in scenarios with imperfect CP and hardware errors, and even outperformed a standard LS channel estimation approach in such scenarios. Moreover, we found that our approach was more resilient to variations in delays, which is crucial considering that delay information may not always be readily available. Overall, our approach simplifies the implementation of RIS-supported OFDM systems by enabling accurate channel estimation without the need for precise phase shift information. The only requirement is a limited signal snapshot, which can be obtained through a brief data transmission at the beginning of each phase, leading to a low overhead. Moreover, our theoretical analysis on the overhead found that our approach outperformed other existing methods, supporting our main claim. The performance enhancement effectively supports the implementation of RIS-supported OFDM systems in practical scenarios with limited knowledge of phase errors. The newly-designed ELM model with an additional target function term offering a concrete method for improving channel estimation in such systems, which was missing in previous research. The other main contribution of this study lies in our ability to train ELM weights optimally using an additional term representing signal values at the target function, which aids in improving the accuracy of channel estimation in such communication systems. The practical effectiveness of this study was also validated through experiments, which were conducted based on the newly-designed models. Furthermore, our proposed approach eliminated the need for delay information through its ability to estimate channels using a limited number of delay values, which greatly reduces the overall overhead. The estimated channel counts were used to determine the degree of overestimation, which was employed to correct estimated phases, while the phase shift vector was found to be the main factor contributing to performance degradation. The practical effectiveness of this study was supported through various real-world data-based experiments, which were conducted while taking into consideration the distinct characteristics of RIS and user devices. We are exploring a specific two-step deformation process of an inline G2 instanton that preserves its isotropy group, applying it to a nearly G2 manifold. In the first step, we define a specific Lie algebra derivative based on an eigenvector of the curvature with a positive real eigenvalue, and we determine that this preserves the G2 instanton. In the second step, any Lie algebra derivative can be added to a regular one, and we establish criteria under which the real eigenvalue remains positive after the first step. Consequently, the deformed instanton still meets the definition of an inline G2 instanton. An alternative approach, referred to as the Nmannifold deformation, is also developed but the constraints on this process are not as well understood. An example demonstrating the existence of G2 instantons on A-bryans spaces and another illustrating non-trivial Nmannifold deformations of G2 instantons on 3-Sasakian manifolds is provided. An elemental analysis of the Nmannifold deformation on 3-Sasakian manifolds reveals that Nmannifold deformations are inherently linked with Killing vectors and appear to be a universal attribute of G2 instantons on three-dimensional homogenous Riemannian manifolds. In addition, an outline is provided for adapting these deformation methods to the hyper-Kahler cone construction. An accompanying graphic illustrates the one-forms and vector fields associated with the Nmannifold deformation on 3-Sasakian manifolds. An research question regarding necessary and sufficient conditions for preserving the G2 instanton property through deformation is posed. Furthermore, an comprehensive list of three-dimensional homogenous Riemannian manifolds is provided. The global COVID-19 pandemic's rapid spread has prompted most countries to adopt a dual strategy of preventing the spread and protecting their healthcare systems. Contact tracing, a key component of this effort, has been utilized to mitigate the outbreak's severity. Recent advancements in mobile technology led to the development of contact tracing COVID-19 apps that aim to complement these efforts by identifying close contacts of infected individuals, facilitating voluntary self-isolation, and preventing hospitalizations. The critical challenge lies in striking a balance between the benefits of these systems, like preserving privacy and preventing potential misuse, and their limitations. Prior research focused on privacy protection primarily relied on well-established methods such as anonymity, privacy preservation, and formal formal verification, and measurement, but these are insufficient to guarantee confidentiality. Our work goes beyond existing research in this area by proposing a method to assess the confidentiality of COVID-19 contact tracing apps' data transmission using statistical analysis techniques. We evaluated two full-featured contact tracing apps operating in Brazil and found that their transmission data could easily be identified, thereby compromising confidentiality. Furthermore, our research revealed that government agencies, advertisers, and hackers could potentially access and utilize this information to undermine the privacy of users. Our findings emphasize the necessity for a formal agreement to be established between users, governments, and other entities to ensure that confidentiality is maintained. They also highlight the need for a detailed, legally binding agreement to ensure that confidentiality is maintained. Our research also offers a set of ground rules for implementing this agreement, providing a framework for achieving this goal. Recent studies indicate that deep neural networks may be able to perform tasks within the limits of quantum systems, and potentially surpass them.  Quantum studies, such as tensor networks, rely heavily on deep neural networks, leading to speculation that quantum systems may contain an implicit deep neural structure that enables them to perform tasks like classify images.  While a direct comparison between quantum and classical systems is complicated, one notable difference is the cost of training: tensor networks require a exponential increase in parameters with the number of qubits, in sharp contrast to the much milder increase in neural networks.  Our study investigates the cost of implementing quantum circuits in neural networks and explores ways to minimize this cost.  Our findings suggest that neural networks can approximate tensor networks with significantly fewer parameters than traditional tensor network methods, often hundreds or thousands of times fewer parameters, making such an approximation a viable approach for embedding quantum systems within neural networks.  These findings imply that it may be feasible to achieve faster classification in quantum systems by translating them to neural networks and to use neural networks to simulate and understand quantum systems, potentially revealing new insights.  Our study outlines the methods for these classifications and presents empirical evidence from various quantum circuits.  Our work ultimately raises the possibility that a neural network representation of a quantum system may reveal new properties that were previously obscured by the complexity of the underlying quantum physics, a phenomenon that holds great promise for future investigations.  Our work is made available through the public repository https://github.com/mjdv/Quantum-data-in-neural-networks. This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems. The tool consists of a converter that uses a shallow embedding of C in ACL2 and is assisted by a pre-built library of functions from the C standard library. The tool also utilizes a set of general-purpose theorem-proving strategies to ensure the generated code is correct. Furthermore, a similar tool for translating ACL2 representations of Java code into Java code using a shallow embedding of Java in ACL2 is described in a companion document. This research relies on a paper titled "A C Standard Library for ACL2" that outlines a collection of ACL2 functions mimicking key C standard library functions. The tool's capabilities are illustrated through its application to several examples, including implementations of the C functions memchr, memrchr, and strcasestr. The tool's source code is available under an open-source license on the repository https://github.com/Coq ACL2/Contributors/shallow-embeddings. The repository contains implementations of shallow embeddings for various programming languages, including C, Java, and Python, as well as a collection of general-purpose theorem-proving strategies, and documentation of the used libraries. Additionally, the tool utilizes the Coq ACL2 bridge (DAKL) library for interacting with Coq. The research behind these contributions is documented in a series of separate studies. This research is primarily focused on the development of a strategy set designed to facilitate the theorem-proving process, which enables the tool to verify the correctness of the generated code. The tool's effectiveness is further demonstrated through its application to more complex examples, including a fully-fledged ACL2 representation of C code for a crash dump analyzer developed in a previous research project, and a partial ACL2 representation of a Java class in a companion document by the author. The generated code is compiled into standalone executable programs, which can be used independently of the ACL2 system. The tool's compilation process relies on a minimal C compiler build specifically for this purpose. The generated code is also distributed alongside the accompanying ACL2 theorems on the repository https://github.com/Coq ACL2/Contributors/shallow-embeddings. The tool's source code is further enriched by the integration of a function tracing mechanism, which allows for the detection of unnecessary ACL2 map functions in ACL2 representations of C code. This feature is used in the tool to minimize the computational overhead associated with the map functions in the generated code.

Building upon Ramanujan's findings for odd zeta values, we investigate similar results for odd Hurwitz zeta functions, which encompass as a special case the Riemann zeta function with odd argument. Our research reveals that no algebraic relation is possible for odd Hurwitz zeta functions, except when the argument is even, in which case it equals a specific combination of the zeta function values at 1, 2, and a fraction of the argument. This work also makes available, using a particular evaluation due to Paris, precomputed tables for Riemann zeta functions at positive even integers up to 22. Utilizing such computations from the algebraic number theory point of view, we contend that the zeta function at 18 equals -1/63, whereas all other relevant possibilities are disallowed through parity and mod 11 consistency constraints. This contrasts with our derived value for the zeta function at 26, which equals -1/963. Both our computation at 18 and the computation at 26 outperform respective limits derived by Ramanujan at 14 and 22. Moreover, our findings for the zeta function at 18 yield the previously uncomputed value of the MZV $(1/2)^3 \ell_2(2/5) \cdot (\frac{3}{2})^3 \ell_1(3/5)$, which equals $-\frac{1}{963}$ in agreement with the relevant finite hypergeometric conjecture by Zagier. This work is further expanded upon in a newly issued technical report. The provided code is accessible at https://github.com/RobertMayer-Schmidt/CZ-data-2022. In a broader context, our work for odd Hurwitz zeta functions can be seen as an implementation of the L-functions and Modular Forms Handbook's "Extrapolation Principle," whereas our specific computation for the zeta function at 26 might foreshadow a future computation for the zeta function at 42 (the case $2s/2+1/2$ is currently under investigation). Ultimately, our work for odd Hurwitz zeta functions contributes to the ongoing effort of determining unknown zeta values at rational points, particularly those related to the Drinfeld-Adrian-Conrey-Diu generalization of the congruent number conjecture. We define a specific version of elliptic cohomology called logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology for finite group representations. This is based on an infinite series of logical circles with the property that their product in the group's action on the representation results in the original representation. The logical circles and their product are represented through a mathematical framework involving the Brauer group of the representation's base field. For a particular representation of the finite group S2, we establish a connection to a mathematical object called Kahn--Liu--Tao theory, resulting in the conclusion that the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology does not rely on the generation of the representation's base field. Moreover, we show that the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology is highly transitive with respect to a particular action on the representation's base field. Consequently, the conclusion is drawn that the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology is an extension of a mathematical object called twisted cohomology, which is transitive with respect to a one-dimensional torus action on the projection of the representation's compactified space CP(V) to a point. Ultimately, the conclusion is drawn that the mathematical object that the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology takes value in is a field extension of the original representation's base field. The work presented here is a part of the author's Ph.D. dissertation, submitted to Carnegie Mellon University. This paper outlines a proposed research initiative where we apply algebraic topology and machine learning together to tackle problems in physics. We argue that a substantial portion of modern physics has its roots in topological ideas and that the intersection of machine learning and topology offers a promising entry point for integrating them into physics. We outline several potential research paths within this domain and provide practical guidelines for getting started at their intersection with quantum physics. This paper serves as a conceptual research initiative precursor, providing a comprehensive background in key technologies and outlining a multi-faceted research approach for a more effective investigation of physics through machine learning and algebraic topology. Furthermore, we suggest establishing a new research community for the fundamental study of physics at their intersection and provide initial research results on a topic that relates to the path integral in quantum mechanics. Specifically, we employ deep learning-based techniques to model path integral representations in quantum mechanics, exploring different geometric and topological configurations as inputs. Our research was inspired by the connections between quantum field theory, topological structures, and machine learning, the principles of which are briefly reviewed in this paper. We aim to contribute towards the incorporation of machine learning and algebraic topology as powerful tools for uncovering new, previously hidden properties of physical systems. We provide various datasets for downloading and deep learning library setup instructions. These instructions, primarily aimed at students and early-stage researchers, offer practical guidance and can serve as a starting point for the proposed research initiative. Therefore, the main body of this paper is primarily descriptive, intended to facilitate entry into this research domain. We hope that our research and these notes can help advance the intersection of machine learning, algebraic topology, and physics. As a result, the background and concepts from computer science, physics, and mathematics, necessary for the proposed research and explained in this paper, are taken for granted but can be assumed known. Our research examined how everyday users and superusers of the Signal privacy-focused messaging service understand the Signal PIN feature. We uncovered that superusers were divided in their understanding of Signal PINs, with some viewing them as a method to confirm device authenticity and others perceiving them as irrelevant. In contrast, non-tech-savvy Signal users were generally unfamiliar with Signal PINs, with many considering them an unnecessary feature. Our findings suggest that introducing new security features may not be effective if users fail to grasp their purpose, with potential solutions involving simplifying security features for all users or leveraging superusers to disseminate security best practices to their counterparts. This research draws from a controlled user testing panel conducted through UserTesting. We explored two specific Signal PIN implementations - Google Android's device verification feature, which uses Signal PINs to confirm device identity, and the Signal app itself, which does not utilize Signal PINs for user authentication. In total, 21 participants took part in, on average, a 60-minute test. We gathered user testing data through unstructured notes and video recordings. The research was conducted by the first author, who is an expert in human-computer interaction, to provide participants with clear instructions and to ensure their comfort during the testing process. Our research adds to the existing literature by contributing to the understanding of security usability through user testing and the research sub-topic of Signal and other communication apps' comprehensibility. We chose the Signal messaging service (previously known as OpenWhisperMail) due to its strong focus on, and numerous awards for, its privacy capabilities. This work addresses the challenge of accurately calculating integrals related to the absorption of solar radiation in the solar energy field, which currently relies on approximate methods like geometric series. We develop a more efficient and precise method based on a new set of absorption coefficients tailored to mimic the solar irradiance spectrum. The resulting quadrature formula enables the exact calculation of a key solar energy integral and offers a simpler alternative to the geometric series method, which has limitations due to its convergence slowing down with increasing energy absorption. Moreover, our method facilitates a straightforward characterization of errors and allows for the optimization of a fundamental parameter, the solar-gamma parameter, to better fit solar irradiance spectra. Employing this optimized gamma value, our method demonstrates excellent agreement with existing approximations for absorbed energy densities but significantly outperforms them in precision, specifically reducing error rates by several orders of magnitude. The proposed technique also shows exceptional performance when simulating solar-cell current-voltage characteristics, surpassing the geometric series method and other approximations with more accurate and reliable results. Notably, when simulated radiation spectra with high gamma values (above 6420 cm-1) are used, our method reveals crucial voltage reduction during simulation, which cannot be captured by the geometric series method or other approximations due to their limited precision. The theoretical foundations and mathematical derivations of our method provide a valuable reference for the scientific community, and its practical applications are highlighted through various industrial cases. Specifically, when put into practice, our method has consistently delivered more accurate simulations compared to existing approximations for several real-world solar cells from diverse manufacturers, and it is expected to enhance the overall simulation quality for a broad range of applications. Ultimately, the most up-to-date version of our method, along with pre-calculated absorption coefficient tables tailored to the AM1.5 solar spectrum, has been made openly available for the scientific community, and its further development is expected to benefit the characterization of solar cells across various real-world radiation conditions. The curvature formed by the Hessian or its generalized Gauss-Newton counterpart has long been an important optimization concept. Despite its utility, obtaining a closed-form solution is only possible in limited contexts. A novel structure known as the ViViT is proposed for the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, allowing for efficient numerical resolution of the Hessian and enabling access to the curvature without substantial computational costs. This is achieved by replacing the conventional Kronecker product framework with a more streamlined diminished structure. Consequently, the complexity of computing the curvature is significantly reduced from cubic to quadratic. This improvement is exemplified through case studies involving convex and non-convex optimization, where the ViViT facilitates curvature-based initialization of stochastic gradient descent and yields more accurate results compared to random initialization. Furthermore, the proposed ViViT enables the substitution of the Hessian with an appoximating matrix, known as the ViViT approximator, in a training dynamics framework commonly used in deep learning. By substituting the Hessian with the ViViT approximator, the complexity of computing the curvature is diminished and training losses are mitigated. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of the ViViT approximator in decreasing training losses and enhancing test accuracy. Overall, the ViViT presents an efficient method for obtaining a curvature matrix with considerable practical applications. The community is invited to utilize the proposed ViViT structure and adopt the curvature-based initialization in their own projects to yield superior performance. In languages that indicate grammatical gender through nouns, co-occurring words are organized around the gender of the initial noun, giving rise to distinct clusters. To investigate how this gender information is represented, we examined the embeddings of adjacent nouns in a corpus from Spanish, exploring the impact of each word's frequency, their relative position, and whether their gender assignment is the same or differs. We found that similar gender between the initial nouns leads to closer proximity in the embedding space, and the most influential factor is typically the frequency of the initial noun. Additionally, we observed that the third word in a sequence is often positioned in a intermediate manner, neither too close to the initial word nor too far away. We based our analysis on the connections between adjacent nouns in trigrams that share the same or opposing genders, and our findings suggest that the system of grammatical gender in languages is not only a characteristic of the vocabulary but also a property of the word representations themselves. We further developed and demonstrated a simple algorithm for generating word embeddings that reflect the syntactic effects of grammatical gender. Our proposed method, which represents clusters of related words as single entities, accurately models the co-occurrence patterns in the corpus and surpasses current state-of-the-art embeddings in semantic evaluation tests. Moreover, by employing ablation studies and controlling for word frequency, we were able to isolate the distinct factors contributing to these cluster representations. We observed that the system of grammatical gender in languages is not only a characteristic of the vocabulary but also a property of the word representations themselves and that the frequency of the initial noun is typically the most influential factor. We were also able to demonstrate through controlled experiments that the model is capturing the effect of grammatical gender rather than other confounding factors such as word homonymy. We discovered that the model is capable of detecting various forms of word relationships, including hypernyms, hyponyms, and opposites, and that it can perform well on similarity and analogy tests. We also showed that the model is resistant to noise during training and can still perform the tasks we specified and that it cannot handle word relationships that rely on subtle meaning distinctions. Estimating the pose of individual objects within images is a significant but complex issue due to the high potential for errors, particularly in scenarios with multiple, partially obscured, or uncommon objects. We tackle this challenge by initially establishing a database mapping class categories to 3D mesh models, allowing the problem to be redefined as a class-level estimation task. Predicting future traffic patterns is essential for multiple roads. Yet, due to a lack of recent data, current methods have significant drawbacks. This research aims to develop a traffic forecasting method that utilizes sparse and delayed data by exploiting similarities between roads. By building upon the understanding that nearby roads typically have similar traffic conditions, we propose introducing spatial relationships into prediction models. Our approach involves three key steps. Firstly, a mixed traffic data regression model is employed to leverage the most relevant sparse data points for each target road. Secondly, the concept of similarity is incorporated into the model's regression matrix. Thirdly, the integration of multiple roads' parallel states allows simultaneous prediction of their respective futures. Our approach was validated on real-world road data and demonstrated improved forecasting accuracy when working with 20% less data and up to 50% delayed data. Its efficacy was further illustrated by processing large datasets in just 0.16 seconds using a typical laptop. The source code can be found at https://github.com/baiky2018/SDFER. This work introduces VACA, a variational graph autoencoder designed to generate counterfactual queries without relying on the causal graph of a dataset. By incorporating constraints from causal graph models into a stable optimization framework, VACA is able to learn a factorized graphical representation of a dataset. We demonstrate that, under certain conditions, the generated counterfactual queries match those from traditional causal inference methods. According to our analysis, VACA is able to identify interventions targeting multiple nodes, address noise and missing data, and achieve robust performance in the presence of random causal noise. Moreover, VACA enables the generation of counterfactual queries for continuous rewards, a task previously thought to be impossible. Our experiments involve simulated and real-world datasets, which show that VACA is able to produce realistic queries that closely match interventions generated by causal models. VACA is available for use under an open-source license at https://github.com/SNLP-Assam/VACA. Additionally, our results can be viewed at http://vaca-assam.github.io. Construction of the Irish LOFAR station has been completed and it's now operating at full capacity. Located strategically at 53.3067$^{\circ}$N 8.0323$^{\circ}$W, the station benefits from minimal light pollution and atmospheric interference due to its remote location on the west coast of Ireland. Observations conducted using the station in its fully configured 11-subarray setup have focused on optimizing its capabilities across the entire frequency range of 0.1 to 10 GHz. These studies, combined with a data analysis tool called the REAL-time Transient Collection backend (REALTA), allow for a fast and efficient processing speed of up to 28 TB of data per day. Real-time observations with REALTA can detect intense signals, like solar flares, at high resolution, and it also enables the creation of dynamic spectra with resolutions of milliseconds and 1 kHz. Furthermore, REALTA can produce accurate peaking flux values for these signals. Finally, the Irish LOFAR station's capabilities have also allowed for a successful search in the fast radio burst (FRB) category with a proven system of detection. With real-time observations at a rate of around 0.2 per hour, the majority of which fall within a 20-kilogramme system, real-time observations with REALTA allow for successful detection of around 0.1 per hour within a 20-kilomegatron system. Moreover, the REALTA system is capable of automatically generating an image using the PSO technique at high resolution and processing speed, and it also enables the creation of a highly accurate light curve using the FASTAPI framework. Using real-time data and the processing speed of the FASTAPI, the REALTA system is capable of automatically creating an accurate classification system. Upcoming research at the Irish LOFAR station includes a greater focus on utilizing the capabilities of the station to gain a more in-depth understanding of pulsars at various levels of activity, expanding upon existing research into transient events like GRBs, searching for and studying FRBs, and investigating the potential for new applications within the field of the Irish LOFAR station. The film industry's massive annual investment is driven by the potential for significant financial return, and understanding which factors influence film profitability can significantly impact a film's financial success. Researchers have explored the impact of certain film characteristics on earnings, but a thorough examination of all factors has not been conducted. Moreover, the lack of comprehensive research on the effects of synchronized releases on film earnings has left an important research gap. To address these gaps, a broader dataset of current films was collected and examined from 2010 to 2019, including 1,518 films, which provided an opportunity to study the effects of multiple film attributes and the financial outcomes of simultaneous film releases. By applying quantitative statistical methods, researchers discovered that the effects of studio, reputation of the film's studio, genre, directed by a female, the number of credited directors, the number of notable actors, and synchronized releases significantly influenced film earnings, which were consistent with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, the research found that the financial outcomes of synchronized releases were negative, indicating a reduced earnings potential for films released during the same time period. Overall, the financial performance of films is influenced by multiple factors, and the decision to release a film concurrently with other movies can significantly impact its financial success. These findings contribute to the understanding of the influence of film attributes and synchronized releases on film earnings, which can aid filmmakers and studio executives in making informed decisions. The research also highlights certain aspects of the film industry that require further investigation. A major strength of this study is its thorough examination of a broader set of film characteristics and releases, which provides valuable insights to the film industry stakeholders. The research's limitation includes its focus on the non-heterogeneous sample of films produced during the specified time interval, which might reduce its accuracy compared to other studies, which analyze a broader set of films. The film dataset used in this research was more than four times larger than other studies, which provides a comprehensive insight into the movie industry's attributes. The research's effectiveness was evaluated through the application of a wide range of dependent variables, including box-office sales, domestic earnings, international earnings, total earnings, score of box-office, and profitable films, which provides a comprehensive analysis of how film attributes influence these variables. The research's effect was evaluated through a thorough examination of a broader set of independent variables, including unique film attributes, which provides a comprehensive insight into the movie industry's attributes. The growing integration of distributed power sources has significantly transformed modern electricity grids, leading to a need for more innovative management strategies to ensure seamless network operation. Existing research has raised the importance of auxiliary frequency regulation in microgrid frequency stabilization, but has neglected the impact of this regulation on voltage stability. This study investigates how implementing frequency stabilization using auxiliary sources within a frequency-based regulation framework affects voltage stability and explores the stability criteria in a simplified model of a microgrid. By analyzing a linearized system around two distinct equilibrium points, one with stable and the other with unstable voltage behavior, we demonstrate the potential of frequency regulation to enhance voltage stability when certain conditions are met. Specifically, we identify the system's ability to transition from an unstable to a stable voltage state and present a control strategy to achieve this transition. Ultimately, we examine the trade-offs between frequency stabilization performance and voltage stability in a frequency-based regulation setting and identify avenues for future research. The findings presented here provide a theoretical foundation for the practical use of frequency regulation to mitigate voltage issues in frequency-based regulation systems. Researchers examine a complex of interconnecting networks, where each unit represents one of two types of networks - electrical or communication. They propose an innovative, simplified model that captures the behavior of an intelligent unit, assuming it can collect and respond to real-time information about its connections. Focusing on this model, they look into the properties of networks that become stable under unit intelligence, using an equilibrium concept to understand their behavior. Additionally, they develop an algorithm to identify specific patterns in these networks, where every unit has direct access to its connections. Further, they investigate the efficiency of units that rely solely on the information they collect, focusing on electrical networks. Finally, they assess a measure of unit intelligence and look into the effects of reducing unit connectivity on this measure in both types of networks, also exploring an alternative version of the model that accounts for unit intelligence variability. They use computational methods and graph theory to analyze these phenomena, exploring a range of scenarios with varying degrees of unit connectivity. Preliminary results indicate that while unit intelligence can be beneficial, it may not always lead to optimal outcomes. Therefore, to gain insights into these phenomena, researchers must explore both unit behavior in the model under focus and network topology. This exploration could contribute significantly to understanding these issues, especially in communication networks, where there has not been much research. Preliminary results indicate that future studies should consider several factors, such as variability in unit intelligence and model extensions to capture dynamics. Blazars are believed to have a unique emission pattern due to a shock wave in their jet, with a specific region causing a significant increase in spectral density in the UV and soft X-ray range. Although this shock wave causes a spectral surge, it has a minimal impact on the level of photon polarization at this spectral band. In a previous study, a specific process, partially polarized inverse external Compton scattering, was examined, and in this research, a modified version of this process involving magnetic fields in shock waves was investigated. Using a specific dataset from the blazar 3C 279 and comparing the results with data from the NuSTAR satellite, it was found that a modified model based on the MAPPIES process can better explain the observed polarization patterns than the standard unpolarized model. The advent of portable micro-camera systems has made available the previously unattainable possibility of capturing light field images. Despite the ease of capturing these images, they are constrained by storage limitations associated with the 4N^2 data structure, where N represents the number of pixels in each spatial direction. Various research studies have sought to address this challenge through optimized coding or structural information extraction methods, but these proposals typically suffer from a lack of portability or comprehensive context, respectively. In an attempt to develop a practical solution, we have created an innovative compression model that is grounded in expert knowledge, specifically designed for common scenes found in everyday life. Our approach's central concept revolves around the idea of 'points of interest,' which are defined as singularities within the image Disparity field and stably predicted using a unique disparity model. Our model, known as KDLM, makes the inherent disparity information explicit and, through expert knowledge integration, is able to reliably detect and locally encode these 'points of interest,' alongside their surrounding Disparity-sensitive micro-variants. Our results demonstrate that the KDLM is capable of 'underlining' the Disparity field in a manner that significantly enhances compression quality compared to the baseline encoder, while also resulting in a substantial decrease in size for the same image quality. Furthermore, our model's performance compared to prior research studies reveals its superiority through superior quality at a given file size or, conversely, significant reductions in size for the same quality benchmark. The provided source code enables users to generate encoded light field images using our Disparity-sensitive model, enabling effortless evaluation of the model and assessment of its performance. Potential applications for the model include future research studies requiring structured light field data. The model's usability and interactivity are also exemplified through the creation of a user-friendly demo that showcases Disparity slipmaps in real-time. This work marks a milestone in the development of a comprehensive understanding of the structure of common natural scenes. Population microdata, readily available in most low and middle-income countries, enables various statistical analysis, notably producing accurate estimates for small areas. Estimating population characteristics in small areas, a core function of statistical offices, can be achieved through two principal approaches: design-based estimators and model-based estimators. Both methods have been developed and refined over time, each with its own advantages and limitations. This research assesses the effectiveness of these techniques in small-area estimation, focusing on a specific design-based approach known as empirical best linear unbiased predictor. The study employs simulated microdata representing a rural district in Nepal, revealing that model-based estimators, such as calibration and post-validation imputation, yield more accurate results. The variance estimates produced by these models demonstrate a 95% confidence level accuracy, underscoring their reliability. Consequently, a decision-making framework is introduced to aid in the selection of suitable small-area estimation methods. Ultimately, this research implies that a combination of both design- and model-based techniques may produce more accurate estimates than either approach used alone. The findings and recommendations presented can benefit national statistical agencies in making informed decisions about the most effective small-area estimation methods to apply. This research has analyzed the existing literature to contribute meaningfully to small area estimation theory and practice.

A long-standing issue related to atmospheric characterization remains largely unresolved, namely, the lack of in-depth studies on how effectively different atmospheric models mimic actual tropospheric profiles. We intend to address this gap by examining the agreement between on-site measured aerosol profiles and those generated by atmospheric models. This paper presents our findings from a pilot study conducted at the Spanish Observatorio de El Teide on the island of Tenerife in March 2019. We compared four atmospheric models – TNOI4, TNOUL4, ARCTIC, and ARCTIC UL, each utilizing the Large Binocular Telescope's observing site data and our own on-site measured aerosol profiles, obtained through continuous monitoring. Our results show notable discrepancies among the four atmospheric models in terms of simulated aerosol profiles and mean vertical aerosol content. We observed significant discrepancies, especially in the ARCTIC scenario where the difference between model predictions and on-site measurements reached as much as three orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the TNOUL4 model demonstrated the smallest disparity with on-site measurements, keeping the difference below one order of magnitude across the entire altitude range. This study provides a comprehensive comparison of atmospheric models in terms of agreement with on-site measurements and paves the way for future studies to utilize these models for atmospheric characterization during observations. Importantly, our study highlights the necessity for in-depth investigations into the underlying algorithms and input parameters of atmospheric models to understand their mechanisms and potentials for simulations. Ultimately, the ultimate goal of this research is to develop efficient atmospheric models that can be used for real-time observations to minimize the impact of atmospheric interference on ground-based observatories. To achieve this objective, the next part of this study will examine the effects of varying atmospheric models on the observations of a selected instrument, namely, the Near-infrared Spectrometer. By exploring this intersection of atmospheric characterization and ground-based observatories, the study aims to contribute new knowledge and facilitate the optimization of atmospheric models for real-time applications. In real-world applications, analyzing time series data requires comprehensive modeling of its multiple dimensions.  This research delves into a phenomenon where seasonal influences are absent from certain time series, a trait that has received little attention. We refer to the practice of discovering and handling varying seasonal patterns as Multi-period Modeling (MPM). The current modeling systems are inadequate for two reasons. Firstly, as the number of possible periods increases, the number of potential models to fit also rises, significantly swelling the computational load. Secondly, the existing traditional statistical models fail to fully exploit data structure similarities across different periods. To address these challenges, we developed the multi-period Analytic Hierarchy Regression model (MPAR), a novel approach that breaks down MPM into separate regression tasks. This allows for an substantial reduction in computational requirements and a more efficient exchange of information across different periods. Furthermore, MPAR is capable of regulating noise within time series data and is adaptable to datasets of any size. Our model takes advantage of sparse regularization developed by Brookes et. al. to enhance the inter-period similarity of Bayesian posterior distributions. The model parameters are optimally determined through 20-strength Starry Night Training. Our research utilizes the mpvar Python library to efficiently handle large datasets. To evaluate MPAR's effectiveness, we conducted numerous quantitative analyses on a range of financial and climate datasets. The results demonstrate that MPAR's approach outperforms established statistical techniques such as SARIMA, with particular success in time series length of only 100 steps. However, the method shows robustness even when considering up to 1000 data steps. The code for mpvar Python library is publicly available on our GitHub page at https://github.com/DesertSky88/mpvar. Federated learning allows diverse clients to co-train a shared model while maintaining ownership of their data, but this benefit comes with new obstacles. The various training times and abilities of clients can result in model biases, potentially exacerbating existing social disparities. Moreover, the lack of control over client data in FL makes it difficult to ensure the security of user privacy, and the challenge of achieving privacy parity among clients further complicates the issue. This paper delves into these issues, examining the problem of equilibrium, identifying key factors that contribute to privacy disparities, and proposing a method for maintaining equality and achieving differential privacy in the context of FL. By modeling client heterogeneity through stochastic models, and considering the impact of local computation on privacy, the authors develop a framework that enables equitable and private model training. This is achieved through the optimization of a dual-objective function that maximizes model accuracy while minimizing bias and privacy discrepancies. By replacing traditional heterogeneity compensation with a compensation mechanism that promotes equity and provides differential privacy, the authors improve the efficiency of FL, enabling its use in scenarios previously excluded from FL research. The framework's effectiveness is supported by numerical simulations and real-world experiments demonstrating its ability to successfully mitigate bias and achieve differential privacy in various scenarios. These results demonstrate the practical applicability of the proposed framework in the context of resource-constrained Internet-of-Things devices. The authors conclude by exploring the broader implications of this work, including its potential to enhance the social and privacy aspects of model training through transfer learning. This highlights the importance of addressing the equity-issue in model collaboration and the need to demonstrate the effectiveness of various justice methods in the context of FL. Moreover, this study demonstrates the potential to use justice methods in the context of FL and encourages the extension of these concepts to edge AI applications. This research contributes to the investigation of intelligent surfaces (IRS) in wireless networks that utilize energy harvesting (EH) to decrease non-linearity and increase non-trivial energy efficiency. To enhance performance, an IRS-aided EH network is examined under a unique linear interference scenario, where an IRS can't directly assist the transmitter. Consequently, a two-layer optimization issue arises: resolving this top-level problem involves determining the optimal jurisdiction of the IRS, while the lower-level problem involves optimizing transmitter and user powers. We initially tackle the top-level problem through an unsupervised machine learning (ML) approach, where ML algorithms are trained to forecast optimal IRS jurisdiction based on diverse channel states. This jurisdiction is then utilized to derive closed-form expressions for optimized transmitter and user powers. A simulation-based analysis confirms that our solution outperforms current benchmarks. Moreover, a low-complexity adaptation of this solution is proposed for cases where ML algorithms encounter difficulties in forecasting jurisdiction due to limited data reception. We demonstrate that this modified solution performs admirably, even in such adverse situations. Furthermore, a comparison with a competing benchmark reveals that our solution is superior, especially when channel changes are frequent. Overall, the performance benefits of this solution are evident, whether working in optimal or suboptimal conditions. This research was funded by the Saudi Arabia build-in. program. We obtained radiative transfer models for three types of gas in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud, fitted to a combined line spectrum from a frequency domain interferometer and a submillimeter continuum map. These gas types include ionized gas, neutral atomic gas, and a photodissociation region. Our analysis reveals that the ionized gas has a scale height of approximately 2.5x10^11 cm and a brightness temperature of around 800 K. It matches the line intensities of key spectral lines relative to their critical densities. However, this agreement is lost at lower densities, indicating self-absorption due to the gas itself. Calculations also suggest that about 40% of the line flux comes from behind the cloud, primarily from the PDR. Despite significant efforts, we were unable to find a single solution that accurately fits the line intensities of all observed transitions. Nonetheless, a subset of lines can be fitted using 2-component models, comprising 1) a cold component (around 25 K) and 2) a warm component (around 150 K). Both components require excess UV radiation of around log($I_V$)/erg cm^-2 s^-1 ~ 1 for neutral atomic species and a smaller fraction for the PDR. Our analysis of SO bandheads suggests that there is no need for a large magnetic field to explain the observed intensity. Rather, it can be attributed to the brightness of the PDR, although the comparison with other data suggests the intensity might be lower than average for such regions. Finally, a search for CO molecules revealed none within the observed frequency range. However, it's possible that CO molecules are present at much lower column densities. Further observations, particularly at the plateaus of the spectral lines, could confirm or rule this possibility. On the other hand, it's also possible that CO molecules could be destroyed by the intense radiation from the nearby star R Oph, a hypothesis that can be confirmed by observing the star's evolution over time. A competing theory is that CO molecules could be broken down into CH+ molecules, which could explain the absence of CO molecules and the high abundance of other species such as CN and CS within the cloud. A more in-depth study into these processes in R Oph's cloud would provide valuable insights into the star's actual age. This research aims to develop an advanced predictive framework for severe illness and death in patients with COVID-19, leveraging data from electronic medical records. The proposed model, known as the Extended Poisson autoregressive with external regressors, or EXPAR model, includes variables that are commonly used to track disease progression and patient well-being. By using a method of factor augmentation, our study demonstrates that incorporating information on hospital stay duration improves the model's performance, especially its ability to predict near-term mortality. Furthermore, we investigate the long-term effects of mortality prediction by expanding the timeline of our analysis to include data from patients who were treated up to two years after their initial admission to the hospital. To enhance the model's reliability, we maintain separate datasets for training and testing purposes, allowing us to evaluate its accuracy using metrics such as the Brier score and the S score. Eventually, our results show that the expanded EXPAR model, which accounts for changes in patient well-being and other time-dependent variables over their hospital stay, performs significantly better compared to earlier models developed by the team. Mortality prediction models like these are expected to support clinical decision-making and facilitate patient monitoring during their hospitalization. Additionally, by demonstrating improved performance over time, these models are expected to contribute substantially to patient care outcomes. Lastly, by indexing patients who are at a high risk of death based on their predicted mortality probability, healthcare providers can implement targeted interventions to enhance recovery chances and ultimately save more lives. Finally, by incorporating the expanded EXPAR model into an decision-making system, clinicians can implement proactive and timely interventions to improve patient outcomes. The potential applications of this research are extensive, and could soon be used to support decision-making in a variety of critical-care situations. The extended versions of this research have been accepted for publication and have been utilized by hospitals to forecast near-term mortality. We define a new type of space called the digitized sphere, created by applying the 1-skeleton process to the half-sphere. This helps us prove that in geodesically complete CAT(0) spaces, all cut points lie on the boundaries formed by this process. This finding allows us to identify the boundaries of such spaces, similar to the way the southern hemisphere of the sphere is defined by points with a positive y-coordinate. We also introduce a new approach for studying spaces with non-truncated boundaries, inspired by the radial trees in the 1-skeleton of the half-sphere. A space with a non-truncated boundary can be expressed as the amalgamated product of a tree and the boundary. This can be repeated, ultimately leading to a proof that a boundary lacking such a tree structure contains only isolated points. This helps us solve Brieux and Zilioto's conjecture, proving that a boundary lacking a tree structure is simply a circle. Ultimately, our method allows us to establish a new connection between a space's boundary and its fundamental group, analogous to the relationship between a number's binary expansion and the 2-skeleton of the hyperbolic plane. Specifically, a space's boundary can be viewed as a branch of its fundamental group, with this branch consisting of a tree. This new idea gives us a thorough understanding of the relationship between a space's boundary and its fundamental group, allowing us to prove that a space's boundary is a circle if its 2-skeleton is a simply connected space. Moreover, our method enables us to demonstrate that a space's boundary is a circle or a quasigeodesic by examining its 3-skeleton. A new method for studying spaces with a non-truncated boundary allows us to prove that a boundary lacking a tree structure contains only isolated points and ultimately that a boundary lacking a tree structure is simply a circle. We demonstrate that our method for studying spaces with a non-truncated boundary is consistent with the known properties of the half-sphere, the northern part of which is a simply connected space, while its 1-skeleton contains all cut points, its 2-skeleton is a simply connected space, and its 3-skeleton is a quasisymmetric space. Consequently, our method for studying spaces with a non-truncated boundary enables us to demonstrate that a space's boundary is a circle or a quasigeodesic. Drawing upon studies in trust assessment in the context of machine translation and the concept of translate-ability, this methodology first establishes a framework for collecting complete data on translation accuracy. Subsequently, reliability is effectively measured using the calculated accuracy probabilities. Moreover, a mechanism for updating reliability estimates in line with current information is developed, enabling the application of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for dynamic assessment. The proposed methodology is illustrated by applying it to evaluations of two translators. Compared to existing evaluation methods, this approach offers clear benefits in terms of simplicity, a clear distinction between sample and population reliability, and the ability to update reliability estimates dynamically. Theoretical discussions are also accompanied by empirical findings from recent studies. The purpose is to enhance the efficiency and credibility of translators through dynamic assessment of their reliability. Firstly, it's possible to measure the amount of energy that's not absorbed by a system using a specific frequency range. Secondly, the total energy absorbed across all possible frequencies equals the total energy available, which is dictated by the incident intensity and the system's input impedance. These discoveries led to the creation of two newinequalities that relate to the energy absorbed in a system, as well as the reliance of this phenomenon on the system's frequency-dependent properties. Ultimately, these findings offer valuable tools for understanding and predicting the energy absorbed in complex scattering media, such as those composed of multiple layers or irregularly-shaped particles. We examine whether the 'winning lottery ticket' phenomenon, which shows that smaller subnets within larger ones have superior performance to the entire net, is prevalent in models that use convolutional layers. Our research suggests this phenomenon primarily exists in nets that use fully-connected layers, and we found that a smaller 'ticket' from a net that uses convolutional layers alongside other layers has worse performance than the entire net, whereas the same 'ticket' from a net that solely uses convolutional layers showed no significant difference in performance compared to the entire net. These findings indicate that trimming certain convolutional layers from a net that uses these layers does not lead to notable improvements in classification accuracy, and thus these layers are likely essential components of the net. Our research also shows that trimming some parameters from 'winning tickets' often results in a net with similar parameters to the entire net, and the best-performing nets have a parameter range that falls within this range. Our research suggests that trimming some parameters from 'winning tickets' obtained through Bayesian Optimization often results in a net with a superior capacity for generalization, and while we found this to be rare with random ticket selection, we obtained an improvement of 1% in the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets with Bayesian Optimization of ticket selection, and an additional 0.5% with random ticket selection, and an additional 0.1% with traditional grid search and optimization. Our research focuses on the effects of trimming parameters from convolutional neural networks on the entire convolutions structure and the entire convolutions spectrum, and the implications of our findings on the task of attribute prediction and classification in vision. Our research also focuses on the task of computer vision and the task of natural language processing and the implications of our findings on the task of NLP. Our research holds promising future research directions for the task of ticket selection and the task of pruning and is conducted within the task of modern deep neural networks and the implications of our findings on the task of future work in the task of pruning and ticket selection. We introduce an innovative anticipated value-based model for lottery tickets that considers both the probability of winning and the expected value of the prize, taking into account the ticket's cost and random outcome uncertainty. This model assesses the anticipated value of a lottery ticket through a straightforward mathematical formula, making it easy to evaluate and compare different tickets. Our research focuses on how the anticipated value changes when the probability of winning and the ticket's cost are modified. Additionally, we employ marketing strategies and customer management techniques to boost the anticipated value for potential buyers, such as setting a limited-time discount or offering an exclusive experience, as well as reaping the benefits for the lottery organizer when the perceived anticipated value exceeds the actual cost for potential buyers, thereby maximizing profits. Our findings and numerical examples are supported by data from various lottery formats across the globe. This research combines theoretical modeling from both discrete and continuous mathematics with a practical, empirical analysis. The paper's conclusion highlights its most significant contributions. Our new t-SNE will take care of your spherical data with care. In fact, we've modeled the probability of data points $x$ within a small ball of radius $\sigma$ using a von Mises-Fisher distribution, which works perfectly because it's based on a symmetric, continuous distribution. To train our customized t-SNE, we've developed a novel loss function in addition to using the original sampling procedure. We tested our method on various 100-dimensional datasets including 3D brain scan data, brain activity data, wind direction data, and COVID-19 data, taking into account both visualization and non-metric pairwise loss evaluation. Compared to the standard t-SNE approach, our method performed significantly better in terms of reconstruction accuracy and visual clarity. You can easily use our method in scikit-learn. In this research, a quantum computing method combining digital and analog components is developed to simulate complex fermionic systems, utilizing a two-component Jordan-Wigner transformation. The digital component handles fermionic creation and annihilation operators, while the analog component handles momentum operators in Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations for specific applications like topological quantum computation. Experiment results from quantum simulations on a 16-qubit superconducting quantum computer are presented to demonstrate its efficacy, specifically in the context of a one-dimensional p- and p'- orbital model incorporating a Rashba-like spin-orbit coupling, a term absent in traditional fermionic models. The findings include the emergence of numerous zero-energy modes, periodic Z2 topological phase transitions, and an overall energy pattern consistent with prior studies on similar systems that employ exact diagonalization. The simulated energy patterns suggest the feasibility of topological quantum computation based on fermionic systems, and the noise level in the digital part of the simulation is shown to be within an acceptable threshold for such computations. Ultimately, the lower-resolution analog component yields the same physical outcomes as its higher-resolution digital counterpart, illustrating the combined digital-analog approach's effectiveness in simulating complex fermionic systems on a quantum computer. The methodology presented can likely be adapted to simulate other fermionic systems, such as the Kitaev model, and potentially other systems, such as bosonic models incorporating a Harper's and Kronig-Penney term. The methodology's primary advantage is its ability to efficiently simulate complex computational models of topological quantum computation without compromising the accuracy of the results. The methodology can likely expand the current scope of quantum simulations on quantum computers, particularly those employing the Jordan-Wigner transformation. The methodology's primary limitations, however, involve the noise level in the digital part and the current limitations of analog computing techniques. The former limitation can likely be addressed by employing evolution-based simulation methods, while the latter limitation can likely be addressed through the development of more sophisticated analog computing methods or the employment of optimization algorithms to mitigate the noise. Our multi-faceted research aims to definitively establish the relationship between remote work and scrum project success.
We analyzed data from 159 software developers to assess the impact of remote work on project success, using team members' personal opinions to evaluate success.
Our findings indicate that remote work has a negative effect on project success, but this effect can be improved with adequate communication and consistency in working hours.
Our research also reveals statistically significant differences in the success of scrum projects with and without remote work.

By doing so, the research validates a hypothesis regarding the steady homotopy stability of these structures across varying chromatic levels and also advances a theoretical framework for defining a putative "chromatic category". Some initial application of the method involved the extended stably defined equivariant cohomology calculus developed from this new concept in homological theory. This work sends a detailed exploration into the interplay between optimal power management and network topology, focusing on interference networks involving $K$ users and specifically those with random user placements. Under the assumption that each user receives a positive rate from some transmitter, we examine the general system in which each transmitter can adjust its transmission power, examining the effects of optimal versus binary power adjustment on capacity and interference in these systems. Interleaved with theoretical analyses, we present concrete examples to validate our findings. Ultimately, this work identifies the upper and lower limits within which the benefits of optimal power adjustment decrease with the number of users in these systems. Specifically, we show these limits to be proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, noting that this is an order of difference for large $K$. Moreover, we conclude by outlining a broad set of conditions under which similar analysis can be applied to more complex systems, including multi-hop networks, networks with composite structure, and more. Further research is anticipated to validate these conditions. 

This work builds on our previous investigations into the effects of optimal versus binary power adjustment on capacity and interference in interference networks, including a prior study published by IEEE TIT.

This shift is also associated with a crucial scaling behavior in the Fock-space propagator, which differs significantly from typical critical scalings observed in one-dimensional critical systems. Unlike those systems where a critical exponent governs the propagator's correlation length, a set of multifractal exponents determines the shift in the correlator's real-space local amplitude by means of conformal field theory, as was initially established for the eigenstate-specific localization transition. In this study, we extend this distinction to the entire many-body localization deconfinement phase transition and establish a similar multifractal-based scaling characterizing the entire phase transition. This scaling can serve as a means to diagnose whether a system is in a critical state or exhibits eigenstate or deconfinement criticality. Moreover, we have discovered that the Fock-space propagator's large eigenvalues follow a Gaussian distribution, unlike the eigenvalues associated with the one-dimensional diffusion process which follow a GOE distribution. This could provide a significant system-size independent benchmark to test and validate numerically a many-body localization deconfinement phase transition model. The outcomes of the study suggest that the distribution of the Fock-space propagator's large eigenvalues can serve as a reliable indicator of whether a system is in a deconfinement phase. The multifractal exponents associated with this indicator decrease systematically with each added particle when counting the number of particles from the tunneling side of the phase transition. Conversely, the exponents increase systematically when counting the number of particles from the non-tunneling side of the phase transition. This indicates a highly non-standard critical scaling associated with the entire phase transition, where the Fock-space propagator's local behavior follows a multifractal symmetry characterizing this phase transition and where the usual critical dimensionality of one is restored only when the largest possible dimensionality of Fock space is achieved. Consequently, the conventional critical dimensionality of one is never achieved in the many-body localization deconfinement phase transition model. Further investigations revealed that the indicator's exponents calculated using two distinct methods, namely the $[m_n]$ and $\{m_n\}$ approaches, display the same systematic behavior with respect to the number of particles. However, the numerical constant associated with the first method that was found to work well in the context of the eigenstate-based localization phase transition, systematically decreases with each added particle

Recent research has demonstrated the potential of quantum machines to outperform their classical counterparts in classifying tasks, even potentially outperforming multi-layer neural networks. However, existing tests of quantum classifiers have focused on data drawn from the same distribution as the training data, and the effects of testing on adversarial samples with significantly different properties have not been thoroughly investigated. In an effort to address this knowledge gap, we developed methods to create quantum equivalents of the DeepFakes human image dataset and a related binary classification problem. Both the quantum and classical approaches to this problem were tested and found to be highly resistant to adversarial samples. Interestingly, our analysis revealed that the quantum classifier exhibited lower accuracy on a subset of samples featuring obvious quantum disturbances against a clean dataset. This outcome can be attributed to the incorporation of a quantum measure of similarity, which tends to overfit these distinct cases. Our research highlights the importance of testing quantum classifiers against samples with significantly different properties and suggests that measures to prevent overfitting are necessary for these scenarios. In addition, our work aims to promote the development of a standardized benchmark suite to facilitate efficient evaluation of quantum machines in real-world applications. This study examines Steklov eigenvalues for nearly spherical domains in Euclidean space. Formulated as the Dirichlet-to-Ne problem, these eigenvalues serve as fundamental frequencies of nearly spherical domains when responding to external stimuli. We demonstrate that like spherical domains, these eigenvalues will occur at specific points, be real-valued, and follow a certain symmetry pattern. Furthermore, we calculate the exact values of these eigenvalues for two types of nearly spherical domains: those based on the half-sphere and those based on the Schwarz manifold. The method of calculation involves expanding the nearly spherical domain using a power series and applying the Dirichlet-to-Ne transformation to this expansion. By doing so, we are able to retrieve the results for the nearly spherical half-sphere, revisit known results for the full sphere, and obtain the results for the Schwarz manifold, which involves applying Schur's linear algebra techniques to a certain infinite matrix. Additionally, we consider the limiting cases of these nearly spherical domains and show that the method of calculation aligns with established results from spherical geometry. Finally, to illustrate the theoretical findings, we present a numerical example of how these eigenvalues behave in nearly spherical triaxial ellipsoids. The method of calculation used in this study can be considered a classical approach that has been widely utilized in geometric PDE research. The nearly spherical half-sphere and Schwarz manifold examples were initially investigated in the author's master's thesis. This study is primarily published as the author's PhD dissertation.
